title: The audit that sat in a drive for a year
description: A finding that is correct, well-evidenced and even praised in a meeting still isn't part of anyone's job until it has an owner, a ticket, a sprint and a deadline — and the practical, low-authority moves that give it the best chance of getting all four.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why praise or agreement in a meeting doesn't make a finding part of anyone's actual work
Identify the concrete steps that turn a delivered report into work a team's own system can see

contentSections.title: Being praised is not being routed

contentSections.body: An audit: 140 findings, every one reproducible, an executive summary read aloud in an all-hands. The CEO calls it, in front of the company, 'exactly the kind of work we need more of.' A retest scheduled for a year later finds the same barriers, in the same places, completely unchanged — including the checkout flow the CEO specifically mentioned by name.

contentSections.scenario: The audit above: correct, well-evidenced, praised publicly by the person with the most authority in the room. A year later, nothing has moved.
contentSections.question: What's the single most likely explanation?

options.label: The findings were never entered into a system anyone's actual job depended on — no ticket, no owner, no sprint, no deadline
Leadership doesn't really value accessibility, whatever was said in the meeting
The findings were too technical for engineers to act on without more explanation

feedback.no-routing: Right. Praise is a reaction to a document, not an instruction to anyone's calendar. A finding that never becomes a ticket, assigned to a person, inside a sprint, with a deadline, is invisible to the system that actually produces shipped work — no matter how correct it was or how warmly it was received.
feedback.not-valued: Maybe, but there's no actual evidence for that here — you have one enthusiastic meeting and one unchanged product a year later, and a much more mundane explanation fits both equally well: nobody's actual job ever included doing anything with this specific document.
feedback.too-technical: Possibly true for a handful of the 140, but it doesn't explain a year of zero movement across a whole product, including findings a competent developer could fix in twenty minutes once assigned. Something stopped this before technical difficulty was ever the obstacle.

contentSections.concept: **A report existing is not the same as a report being someone's job.** Praise, agreement and even genuine enthusiasm in a meeting are reactions to a document — they are not, by themselves, a ticket, a named owner, a sprint slot or a deadline. Until a finding has all four of those, it isn't part of anyone's actual work. It's a PDF.

contentSections.body:
It's worth noticing how differently a normal software bug enters a team's workflow. A tester finds it and files it directly in the tracker the team already uses. A production error pages someone on call. A code reviewer leaves a comment that blocks the merge until it's addressed. In every case, the system the team's actual work runs through sees the problem automatically.

Most accessibility audits arrive by a completely different route: a standalone document, in a different tool than the team's tracker, addressed to no specific individual, with no due date attached. The tracker that decides what gets worked on this sprint has no idea the audit exists unless a human being manually moves each finding into it — and that manual step is exactly the one that, in the story above, never happened.
A correct finding with no owner, no ticket and no deadline is not part of anyone's job. It's a document.

contentSections.title: Making a document routable

contentSections.body: The fix, in the boring, mechanical sense, doesn't require any authority you don't already have: don't leave the findings sitting next to the team's workflow. Put them inside it.

contentSections.scenario: A team is about to deliver an accessibility audit to a client whose developers already run every other piece of work through their own Jira board.
contentSections.question: Which of these actually raise the odds this audit gets acted on, and which don't help?

items.label: Filing each finding as its own ticket directly in the client's existing tracker, not just attaching a PDF
Suggesting, per ticket, which existing team or role is the natural owner — even without the authority to assign it yourself
Making the written report substantially longer and more detailed, to leave nothing in doubt
Asking in the delivery meeting for a specific date by which the highest-severity tickets will at least be triaged — not fixed, just triaged
Adding a second and third WCAG citation to each finding, for extra rigour

explanation.tickets: This is the single highest-leverage move available, and it costs you time, not authority. A finding inside the tracker is visible to sprint planning by default; a finding in a PDF is invisible by default.
explanation.owner-suggestion: You don't need the power to assign it — naming a plausible owner removes a small decision that would otherwise stall the ticket in an unowned queue, sometimes for months, before anyone even decides whose problem it is.
explanation.longer-report: Length adds reading time, not action. Past the point the finding is already reproducible and specific, more detail doesn't move it closer to a sprint — it moves it further, because longer documents get skimmed, not routed.
explanation.deadline-ask: Triage, not a fix commitment, is a small, specific, sayable-yes-to ask, and it puts a date on the calendar where none existed. A date for triage is what turns 'we'll look at this sometime' into an actual event.
explanation.more-citations: A finding is already actionable once it names what's wrong, where, who it affects and what to do. A third citation adds rigour to an argument nobody was making — it doesn't get anyone closer to opening the ticket.

contentSections.synthesis: None of these four changes require the client to agree to fix anything. They require the client's own existing systems to be able to see that the work exists at all — a much lower bar than 'agree to fix it,' and the one that's actually being missed in the story that opened this lesson.

contentSections.body: Nothing here requires authority you don't have. The move is reducing how many separate, manual steps a finding must survive between 'someone read this' and 'it's in someone's actual sprint' — every one of those steps is a place work quietly stops.

title: Nobody owns it: the accountability gap
description: Why a values statement, a Slack channel and one generous volunteer are not the same thing as ownership — and what a role has to actually hold before accessibility work has anywhere real to land.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish genuine ownership of accessibility work from indicators that only look like ownership
Identify what authority and accountability a named owner needs in order for the role to function

contentSections.title: Everyone thinks it's someone else's job

contentSections.body: A findings review call, four honest answers in a row: engineering says 'that's a design decision.' Design says 'we built to what engineering shipped.' Product says 'legal signed off on the accessibility statement.' Legal says 'we relied on the vendor's compliance claim.' Nobody is lying. The barrier is still there.

contentSections.scenario: A company's website lists 'accessibility' as one of its stated values. A Slack channel, #a11y-questions, exists, and one engineer occasionally answers questions there in her spare time, unpaid, with no formal role or budget attached to it.
contentSections.question: Who owns accessibility at this company?

options.label: The engineer who answers questions in the Slack channel
Nobody — a channel and one person's unpaid goodwill is not the same thing as ownership
Legal, since accessibility is a compliance requirement

feedback.engineer: She's doing real, generous work, and it's exactly the kind of work that quietly stops the moment she changes teams, goes on leave, or simply runs out of spare hours — because nothing about her role actually requires or funds it. That fragility is the tell that this isn't ownership.
feedback.nobody: Right. Ownership means a role with the authority to prioritise the work and the accountability if it doesn't happen. A values statement and a volunteer-run channel provide neither — they provide the appearance of coverage, which is worse than no coverage, because it stops anyone else from noticing the gap.
feedback.legal: Legal can require that certain claims be true and can be exposed if they aren't — but 'exposed if a claim is false' is not the same as 'responsible for making the claim true.' Legal owns the statement's accuracy, not the engineering work that would make it accurate.

contentSections.concept: **Ownership means a named role with the authority to prioritise the work, and the accountability if it doesn't happen.** A mission statement, a Slack channel, or one person's spare-time generosity can look like coverage from a distance. None of them survive the person leaving, the workload changing, or anyone actually asking 'whose job was this, on paper, before today.'

contentSections.body: This is why 'raise awareness' rarely closes an accountability gap on its own. Awareness changes what individuals believe; it doesn't change whose job description includes the work, whose performance review reflects whether it happened, or whose calendar has time blocked for it. Those three things — job description, review criteria, protected time — are the actual load-bearing parts of a role. A campaign that raises everyone's awareness without touching any of the three has changed the mood in the room and left the accountability gap exactly where it was.
Ownership is a role with the authority to prioritise the work and the accountability if it doesn't happen — not a value, a channel, or one person's goodwill.

contentSections.title: What real ownership actually looks like on paper

contentSections.body: A real handbook, a real line, quoted without changing a word: 'Accessibility is everyone's responsibility. All team members are expected to consider accessibility in their work.'

contentSections.code:
From the engineering handbook, section 4.2:

"Accessibility is everyone's responsibility.
All team members are expected to consider
accessibility in their work as part of our
shared commitment to inclusive design."
contentSections.question: This policy line is sincerely meant and widely repeated across organisations. What's actually wrong with it as a mechanism for getting accessibility work done?

options.label: 'Everyone's responsibility' with no named role, budget, or review criteria functions, in practice, as nobody's responsibility
It should specify which WCAG version and conformance level applies
It doesn't mention assistive technology by name

feedback.everyone-nobody: Exactly. When a task belongs to everyone equally, no individual's performance review, workload, or deadline is affected by whether it gets done — which means, in practice, that whoever is already the busiest quietly deprioritises it first, every time, and nobody is accountable for that outcome because the policy never named anyone.
feedback.wcag-version: A specific standard would make the policy more precise about *what* good looks like, but it wouldn't fix the actual mechanism problem: even a precise standard, assigned to 'everyone,' still has no individual whose job is affected by whether it's met.
feedback.no-at: True but beside the point — the flaw here isn't about missing technical detail. It's structural: the sentence creates an expectation with no accountable owner behind it, and that would be just as true if it named every assistive technology in existence.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A responsibility distributed evenly across everyone is, functionally, owned by no one — because nobody's specific job, calendar, or performance review depends on it happening. A working version replaces 'everyone' with a name or a role: *'The platform team's accessibility lead reviews all new components against WCAG 2.2 AA before release, with 10% of the team's sprint capacity reserved for remediation.'* That version has someone whose job is affected if it doesn't happen — which is the only version of 'responsibility' that reliably survives a busy quarter.

contentSections.body: A responsibility given to everyone equally, with no name, no budget and no review criteria attached, is a responsibility given to no one — sincerely meant, and still functionally unowned.

title: Competing with the roadmap on the roadmap's terms
description: A remediation plan kept as its own separate list competes, rarely and as a whole programme, against work with harder deadlines — and loses. The same fixes, sized and entered as ordinary tickets, compete instead against feature work of similar size, far more often.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why accessibility fixes kept as a standalone list get scheduled less often than the same fixes entered as normal sprint tickets
Rewrite a remediation item in the sizing and framing a sprint planning process already responds to

contentSections.title: A separate list is a list that loses

contentSections.body: A 40-item accessibility remediation plan sits in its own spreadsheet, reviewed once a quarter, competing for a fixed '10% of capacity set aside for tech debt' against a payment-provider migration and a security patch backlog. It loses, tidily, every quarter, and nobody in the room is being dishonest about their priorities.

contentSections.scenario: The 40-item plan above stays in its own quarterly-review spreadsheet, competing as a whole programme against security and payment-migration work for a fixed 10% tech-debt slice.
contentSections.question: Across two full quarters, roughly how many of the 40 fixes would you guess actually get scheduled and shipped, kept in this format?
contentSections.explanation: In remediation programmes run this way, the real number is usually in the low single digits — not because anyone decided accessibility mattered less, but because a separate list has to win an infrequent, all-or-nothing competition against work with harder deadlines: a security patch has a CVE number and an auditor asking about it by name; the accessibility spreadsheet has neither. The same 40 fixes, sized in the team's normal estimation units and entered as ordinary tickets in the sprints already touching the affected code, ship at a completely different rate — often ten times faster — because each one now competes individually against feature work of a similar size, on the same terms everything else in the sprint is judged by.

contentSections.body: The lesson isn't 'stop tracking remediation as a set' — a programme view is genuinely useful for reporting overall progress. The lesson is where the individual fix actually competes for a developer's time. That competition happens in sprint planning, ticket by ticket, using the team's own units — story points, t-shirt sizes, whatever they already use — not in a quarterly steering meeting using a unit ('an accessibility programme') that nothing else in the organisation is measured in. A fix that never enters the first competition never gets the chance to win it.

Fixes kept as their own programme compete rarely, as a whole, against work with harder deadlines, and usually lose. The same fixes, sized and entered as ordinary tickets, compete far more often — and mostly win.

contentSections.title: Pitching a fix in the roadmap's own language

contentSections.body: Two tickets, same underlying fix — a missing accessible name on a component used across eleven screens. One gets picked up in the next sprint planning session. The other sits for four months.

contentSections.scenario: Ticket A: 'Accessibility issue #14: fix component per audit finding.' No estimate, no acceptance criteria, tagged 'accessibility,' assigned to no one. Ticket B: 'Add accessible name to Button component (used on 11 screens incl. checkout) — 3 points, acceptance: NVDA announces the button's visible label; component tests updated.' Estimated, has acceptance criteria, named after the actual affected component.
contentSections.question: What's the mechanism behind B getting picked up and A not?

options.label: B is a smaller, easier fix than A
B is written in the exact shape sprint planning already knows how to evaluate and slot in — estimate, acceptance criteria, named component — while A gives planning nothing to act on
B happens to affect checkout, which is simply a higher-traffic page

feedback.smaller: They could be identical in actual effort — the difference here isn't size, it's legibility. Sprint planning slots work in by comparing tickets in a shape it already recognises, and A doesn't offer that shape at all.
feedback.shape: Right. Sprint planning is a process for comparing and slotting in tickets that look like the tickets it already handles — estimated, with acceptance criteria, named after a real component. A ticket missing all three isn't rejected; it's simply unreadable by the process, and unreadable tickets don't get picked, they get skipped past.
feedback.traffic: Checkout being high-traffic is a real point in B's favour once it's actually being considered — but it can't be weighed at all if the ticket is never legible enough to reach that comparison in the first place, which is A's actual problem.

contentSections.mechanism: **A ticket has to be shaped like the other tickets the process already compares before its content can matter at all.** Estimate, acceptance criteria and a named, real component are not decoration — they're the interface a sprint planning process reads through. A finding that skips that shape, however correct, is invisible to the comparison, not weighed and rejected by it.

contentSections.body: Write the fix in the shape sprint planning already knows how to compare — estimate, acceptance criteria, the real component name — and let it win or lose on the same terms as everything else. Skip that shape, and it never reaches the comparison at all.

title: Compliance theatre and how to recognise it early
description: A badge, a boilerplate VPAT and a 100%-completion training rate can all exist alongside zero actual remediation. The tells that separate real evidence of accessibility work from a performance of it — and why noticing early matters more than noticing after your own name is attached to the audit.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the specific tells that distinguish compliance theatre from genuine evidence of remediation
Recognise theatre early enough to avoid becoming the exhibit that makes it look credible

contentSections.title: The badge, the statement, and what's underneath

contentSections.body: A company's site footer proudly links an 'accessibility certified' badge from a third-party vendor. Nobody currently employed at the company can say what was actually tested, by whom, when, or against which assistive technology — the person who commissioned it left eighteen months ago.

contentSections.code:
Voluntary Product Accessibility Template (VPAT)
Conformance Level: WCAG 2.1 Level AA — Full

1.1.1 Non-text Content .......... Supports
1.3.1 Info and Relationships ..... Supports
1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) ......... Supports
2.1.1 Keyboard .................. Supports
2.4.7 Focus Visible .............. Supports
[ ... 42 more criteria, all marked Supports ... ]

No test date. No named tester. No
methodology section. No exceptions listed.
contentSections.question: This is a real, common shape for a VPAT to arrive in. What's the actual tell that this is theatre rather than evidence?

options.label: There's no evidence of what was tested, how, when or by whom — and every criterion marked 'Supports' with zero exceptions is itself implausible for a real product of any complexity
It should say 'WCAG 2.2' instead of '2.1', since that's the newer version
VPATs should never claim Level AA — only Level A is realistic

feedback.no-evidence: Right on both counts. A real, tested product of any real complexity almost always has *some* exceptions — genuine full conformance across 40+ criteria with zero caveats is a red flag on its own, and the complete absence of a test date, tester or methodology means there is nothing behind the document that could actually be checked.
feedback.wrong-version: Using an older WCAG version is a real, separate issue worth flagging, but it isn't what makes this document theatre — a VPAT tested rigorously against 2.1 would still be genuine evidence. The problem here is the total absence of anything checkable behind the claims, at any version.
feedback.level-a-only: Level AA conformance is a completely normal, achievable target and plenty of real products meet it — the flaw isn't the level claimed, it's that nothing in the document lets you verify the claim.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A VPAT is only as good as what's behind it: who tested, when, against which assistive technology and browser combinations, and — almost always, for anything genuinely tested — what the honest exceptions are. A document with 'Supports' on every line, no date, no tester and no methodology section isn't evidence of conformance. It's a claim shaped like evidence, and the shape is the whole tell.

contentSections.body: A VPAT or a badge is only as good as what's checkable behind it — who tested, when, against what, and what the honest exceptions were. Zero exceptions across 40+ criteria is a red flag, not a good sign.

contentSections.title: Catching it before you're the exhibit

contentSections.body: The riskiest moment isn't when a company is doing nothing. It's when a company is doing just enough — a badge purchased, a training completed — that a real auditor's name on the engagement starts reading, to the outside world, as confirmation the badge was earned.

contentSections.scenario: A prospective client tells you, honestly and without spin, about their accessibility programme so far: a checkbox training every employee completed last year (100% completion), a purchased third-party 'accessibility certified' badge with no report attached, and a public statement whose wording is nearly identical to a competitor's, with the company name swapped in.
contentSections.question: Which of these are signs of a genuine programme, and which are signs of theatre?

items.label: 100% completion of a one-time checkbox training, with no follow-up and no one's incentives tied to acting on what was learned
A purchased badge with no accompanying test report available on request
A public accessibility statement whose wording is nearly identical to a competitor's, with only the company name changed
Asking, before signing anything, whether an actual test report exists behind any of these and offering to review it

explanation.training: Training raises awareness at one moment in time. Without follow-up, and without anyone's workload or review reflecting whether it changed anything, it's a completion statistic, not a programme — this is the same gap named earlier for handbook language, in a different costume.
explanation.badge: A badge with no report behind it is a claim dressed as a credential. It tells you someone paid a vendor; it tells you nothing about what, if anything, was actually tested.
explanation.copied-statement: Copied wording is close to a confession that nobody actually assessed this company's own product — a genuine statement, even a short one, tends to name something specific to the actual product it describes.
explanation.ask-for-report: This is the one real diagnostic available to you before you commit your own name to anything: a company with genuine work behind its claims can usually produce something — a report, a set of findings, a name of who did the testing. A company that can't produce anything is telling you, indirectly but clearly, what you're about to become part of.

contentSections.synthesis: None of the first three tells you anything is fixed. All three are compatible with zero actual remediation. The fourth — simply asking for the report and seeing what exists — is the cheapest, earliest check available, and it's worth running before your own name appears anywhere near the engagement, not after.

contentSections.body: Training completion, a purchased badge and a copied statement can all coexist with zero real remediation. Asking whether a checkable report actually exists, before your name is attached to anything, is the cheapest way to find out early.

title: Finding the person who can actually decide
description: A proposal can get enthusiastic nods from everyone in the room and still go nowhere, because none of them control the budget line it needs. Mapping who actually holds that authority, and turning a diffuse ask into one a specific person can say yes to.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish roles that can advocate for a fix from the role that can actually fund or schedule it
Compose a specific, decision-shaped ask addressed to the person who actually holds that authority

contentSections.title: The decision doesn't live where the meeting is

contentSections.body: A remediation proposal gets enthusiastic nods from the head of design, the engineering lead and a product manager, in a meeting everyone agrees went well. Three months later, nothing has moved — because none of the three people in that room controlled the budget line the fix actually needed.

contentSections.scenario: A multi-sprint remediation effort needs both engineering capacity and sign-off that it's worth prioritising over other roadmap work. Three candidates: an engineering manager, who can reshuffle their own team's sprint but has no authority to add headcount or move dates on committed features; in-house legal counsel, who can require the company take action and flag risk, but doesn't control any product budget; and the VP of Product, who owns the quarterly roadmap and the budget allocated against it.
contentSections.question: Which of these three should the ask actually be addressed to, first?

options.label: The engineering manager — they're closest to the actual work
Legal counsel — they can require it, which is the strongest form of authority
The VP of Product — they're the one who can actually allocate roadmap capacity and budget against a multi-sprint effort

feedback.eng-manager: The engineering manager is a genuinely useful ally and can move small things fast — but for a multi-sprint effort that competes against committed roadmap items, they don't hold the authority to make that trade-off. That decision sits above them.
feedback.legal: Legal's authority is real but narrow: they can create pressure to act and flag exposure, which is valuable leverage to bring *to* the actual decision-maker — but legal doesn't hold a product budget or roadmap capacity to allocate.
feedback.vp-product: Right. A multi-sprint effort is, functionally, a roadmap and budget decision, and the VP of Product is the role in this scenario who actually holds both. Everyone else can support the case, but the yes has to come from here.

contentSections.concept: **The right person to ask isn't the one closest to the work or the one with the loudest formal authority in general — it's the one who specifically holds the resource the ask requires.** Sprint capacity, roadmap priority and budget are often controlled by different people, and a proposal addressed to the wrong one of the three can get genuine enthusiasm and still go nowhere, because enthusiasm isn't the resource being requested.

contentSections.body: Mapping this doesn't require an org chart from HR. It requires one honest question about each candidate: if they said yes right now, would anything actually change? An engineering manager saying yes changes what their team works on next sprint — real, but small and reversible. A VP of Product saying yes changes what's on the roadmap for the quarter — the actual scale a multi-sprint programme needs. The person whose yes changes the least is usually the easiest to get a meeting with, which is exactly why so many proposals stop at the wrong desk.
Ask the person who holds the specific resource the fix requires — sprint capacity, roadmap priority or budget — not the person closest to the work or the one it's easiest to get a meeting with.

contentSections.title: Making the ask specific enough to say yes to

contentSections.body: Even addressed to the right person, 'please prioritise accessibility' is not a request anyone can say yes to in a single reply — there's no decision in it small enough to make.

contentSections.intro: You've identified the VP of Product as the person who can actually allocate the capacity a remediation effort needs. Build the ask, one field at a time.

fields.prompt: Who is this addressed to?
options: Whoever reads the shared accessibility channel
The VP of Product, by name
The whole leadership team, cc'd
fields.correctValue: The VP of Product, by name
fields.feedback: A request with no single named recipient has no single person accountable for replying to it — it becomes everyone's optional read and no one's specific task.

fields.prompt: What's the actual decision being requested?
options: Prioritise accessibility this quarter
Allocate one engineer at 50% capacity for two sprints to fix the eight Blocker-severity findings from the recent audit
Fix the accessibility issues
fields.correctValue: Allocate one engineer at 50% capacity for two sprints to fix the eight Blocker-severity findings from the recent audit
fields.feedback: This is a decision sized to fit inside a single meeting or reply — a specific resource, a specific duration, a specific, bounded scope. 'Prioritise accessibility' isn't a decision at all; it's a mood.

fields.prompt: What evidence backs the size of the ask?
options: A general statement that accessibility matters
The eight findings' severity ratings and which specific user journeys they block, cited directly from the audit
A comparison to what competitors publicly claim
fields.correctValue: The eight findings' severity ratings and which specific user journeys they block, cited directly from the audit
fields.feedback: Evidence tied directly to the specific ask — these eight findings, this much blocked journey — lets the VP evaluate the actual trade-off. General statements about importance don't help them size anything.

fields.prompt: What's the actual ask for a response?
options: No deadline — better to let them think it over
A yes/no by a specific date, tied to the next sprint planning cycle
A deadline of 'as soon as possible'
fields.correctValue: A yes/no by a specific date, tied to the next sprint planning cycle
fields.feedback: A date tied to a real, existing event on their calendar — the next sprint planning cycle — gives the ask a natural deadline that doesn't feel arbitrary, and makes silence itself become visible as a choice.

contentSections.synthesis: Put together: *"[VP name] — the recent audit found eight Blocker-severity findings blocking checkout and account recovery for screen reader and keyboard users. Fixing them needs roughly one engineer at 50% for two sprints. Could you let me know by [date, before next sprint planning] whether that capacity can be allocated?"* Named recipient, sized decision, specific evidence, real deadline — four things a general appeal for prioritisation never has.

contentSections.body: A decision-maker can only say yes to something sized small enough to be a decision — a named recipient, a specific resource and duration, evidence tied directly to that size, and a real deadline. 'Please prioritise this' has none of the four.

title: Practice — Diagnose the Blocker in Seven Stalled Programmes
description: Seven short scenarios, each a real-shaped version of an accessibility programme that stalled. No new concepts — this is where naming the actual blocker stops being something you recognise in a lesson and becomes something you can do cold, on an unfamiliar case.

learningObjectives.text: Diagnose which organisational blocker — routing, ownership, roadmap competition, theatre or no decision-maker — explains a stalled programme
Distinguish a real accountability or routing mechanism from something that only resembles one

contentSections.title: Seven drills

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Seven scenarios across the module's four blockers — no routing, no ownership, losing to the roadmap, and theatre — plus one on finding the decision-maker. Do them in one sitting or spread across three; nothing here expires or is timed.
If a drill needed a hint, that's the thing to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Diagnose Why One Real Audit Didn't Ship
description: Take an accessibility audit you have real knowledge of — one you wrote, one from a past job, or a public one with a documented aftermath — and produce a diagnosis naming the actual blocker and the one intervention most likely to move it, instead of a general call to try harder.

learningObjectives.text: Reconstruct what actually happened to a real set of findings after delivery
Diagnose the primary organisational blocker using evidence rather than assumption
Propose a specific, addressed, sized intervention rather than a general recommendation

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Every audit that stalled had a reason, and the reason is almost never 'nobody cared.' It's one of a small number of mundane, specific, fixable mechanisms — and naming the right one is worth more than a second, more thorough audit of the same product.

contentSections.title: Diagnose why one real audit didn't ship
contentSections.brief: Pick a real accessibility audit whose aftermath you actually know something about — one you conducted yourself, one from a past role, or a public case with a documented follow-up (a published retest, a news story about an unresolved lawsuit, a case study). If you genuinely have no real case available, construct a detailed, realistic one from a product and organisation you know well enough to reason about specifically — generic placeholders won't survive this lab's stages.
contentSections.deliverable: A diagnosis naming the blocker and a specific intervention: a reconstructed timeline, a primary-blocker diagnosis backed by evidence from that timeline, and one specific, addressed, sized intervention.

stages.title: Reconstruct the timeline
stages.instructions: Write out what actually happened after the findings were delivered — as concretely as you can reconstruct it. Who received the report first? What was said about it in the next meeting, if there was one? Did any finding ever appear in a tracker, a ticket, a sprint? What's the current state, today? Where you genuinely don't know something, say so explicitly rather than guessing — 'unknown whether it ever reached engineering' is more useful than a confident invention.
stages.checkpoint: You have a timeline with at least four real, dated or sequenced events, and every gap in your knowledge is marked as a gap rather than filled in.

stages.title: Diagnose the primary blocker
stages.instructions: Using the four blockers from this module — no routing, no real ownership, losing to the roadmap, compliance theatre — decide which one the timeline most supports as the *primary* cause. More than one may be partly true; name the one your evidence most directly points to, and say why the others fit less well. Cite specific events from your timeline, not general impressions.
stages.checkpoint: You've named one primary blocker, backed by at least two specific pieces of evidence from your own timeline, and explicitly ruled out at least one plausible alternative.

stages.title: Write the specific intervention
stages.instructions: Write the one concrete move most likely to actually restart this — addressed to a named person or role (using the mapping approach from lesson five), sized small enough to be a real decision, with evidence attached and a specific ask for a response by a date. This is not a general recommendation ('leadership should prioritise this') — it's the actual message or ticket you would send, today, if you had the chance.
stages.checkpoint: Your intervention names a specific addressee, a specific sized ask, attached evidence, and a real deadline — and it follows directly from the blocker you diagnosed in stage two, not from a generic playbook.

rubric.criterion: The timeline is specific and honest about its gaps
rubric.meets: Real events, roughly dated or sequenced, with genuine unknowns marked as unknowns rather than invented.

rubric.criterion: The blocker diagnosis is evidence-based, not assumed
rubric.meets: Names one primary blocker, cites at least two specific pieces of supporting evidence from the timeline, and explicitly rules out at least one alternative.

rubric.criterion: The intervention is addressed to a specific person or role
rubric.meets: Not 'the company' or 'leadership' — a named person or a specific, real role, matched to the resource the intervention actually needs.

rubric.criterion: The intervention is sized to be a real, sayable-yes-to decision
rubric.meets: A specific scope and duration or effort estimate, not an open-ended request to 'prioritise accessibility.'

rubric.criterion: The intervention follows from the diagnosis
rubric.meets: A routing problem gets a routing fix; a roadmap-competition problem gets a resizing fix — the intervention isn't a generic recommendation bolted onto whichever blocker was found.

contentSections.body: A diagnosis that names the mechanism and a move sized to fit inside one real decision is worth more than a longer list of everything that's wrong.

title: Checkpoint — Why Correct Findings Don't Get Fixed
description: Ten questions, all from this module. Each course is sold separately, so nothing here draws on other courses. Ungraded, untimed, and getting one wrong just means it comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's diagnostic frame: ownership, the sprint-ticket route, compliance theatre, and who can decide, without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Why Correct Findings Don't Get Fixed

questions.from: This module — Why Correct Findings Don't Get Fixed
questions.prompt: An audit is praised publicly by a CEO. A year later, nothing has changed. What's the most likely explanation?

options.label: The findings were never entered into a system anyone's actual job depended on — no ticket, owner, sprint or deadline
The CEO's praise was insincere
The findings were too technical to act on

questions.explanation: Praise is a reaction to a document, not a ticket, owner, sprint or deadline — until a finding has all four, it isn't part of anyone's actual work.

questions.from: This module — Why Correct Findings Don't Get Fixed
questions.prompt: What does real ownership of accessibility work require, beyond a values statement or a volunteer-run Slack channel?

options.label: A named role with the authority to prioritise the work and the accountability if it doesn't happen
Company-wide awareness training
A public accessibility statement

questions.explanation: A value, a channel or a statement can all exist alongside zero accountability. Real ownership needs a name attached to authority and consequence.

questions.from: This module — Why Correct Findings Don't Get Fixed
questions.prompt: Why do accessibility fixes kept in their own separate quarterly-review spreadsheet usually get scheduled far less often than the same fixes entered as normal sprint tickets?

options.label: They compete as a whole slow-moving programme against work with harder deadlines, instead of ticket-by-ticket against similarly sized work every sprint
Developers don't want to fix accessibility issues
Spreadsheets are a worse tool than trackers for any kind of work

questions.explanation: The format of the competition, not developer willingness or the tool itself, is what changes the odds — a rare, high-stakes competition versus a frequent, similarly-sized one.

questions.from: This module — Why Correct Findings Don't Get Fixed
questions.prompt: A VPAT has 'Supports' marked for every single criterion, with no test date, tester or methodology listed. What's the honest read?

options.label: A claim shaped like evidence, with nothing checkable actually behind it
Strong proof of full conformance
Fine, as long as the company is reputable

questions.explanation: Zero exceptions across dozens of criteria, with no way to check who tested what or when, is a tell for theatre, not a sign of thoroughness.

questions.from: This module — Why Correct Findings Don't Get Fixed
questions.prompt: A client reports 100% completion of a one-time checkbox accessibility training, with nothing after it. What does that figure show?

options.label: Strong evidence that staff now apply accessibility in their work
A completion statistic, which is not the same as a programme
Proof that the barriers in the product have now been fixed

questions.explanation: Training raises awareness at one moment in time. Without follow-up, and with nobody's workload or review reflecting whether it changed anything, it is a completion statistic and not a programme.

questions.from: This module — Why Correct Findings Don't Get Fixed
questions.prompt: Why does raising awareness rarely close an accountability gap on its own?

options.label: People forget campaign messages within a week of seeing them
Campaigns are priced beyond what most teams can afford to run
It leaves job descriptions, reviews and protected time unchanged

questions.explanation: Job description, review criteria and protected time are the load-bearing parts of a role. A campaign can change the mood in the room and leave the gap where it was.

questions.from: This module — Why Correct Findings Don't Get Fixed
questions.prompt: Two tickets describe the same fix. Ticket A reads 'Accessibility issue #14: fix component per audit finding' with no estimate. Ticket B names the component, has 3 points and has acceptance criteria. Why does B get picked up?

options.label: It is a smaller and easier fix than ticket A would be to do
It matches the shape sprint planning already knows how to compare
It touches checkout, which is a higher-traffic page than A's

questions.explanation: Sprint planning compares tickets that look like the ones it already handles. A ticket with no estimate, no acceptance criteria and no named component is not rejected, it is skipped past.

questions.from: This module — Why Correct Findings Don't Get Fixed
questions.prompt: A company's public accessibility statement is nearly identical to a competitor's, with the company name swapped in. What does that suggest?

options.label: Nobody assessed this company's own product before writing it
The company applies the same tested standard as its rival
The statement is safer since a competitor already vetted it

questions.explanation: Copied wording is close to a confession that nobody assessed this company's own product. A genuine statement tends to name something specific to the product it describes.

questions.from: This module — Why Correct Findings Don't Get Fixed
questions.prompt: Whom should you ask for a fix that needs sprint capacity, roadmap priority or budget?

options.label: The person closest to the daily work on the page itself
The person who holds the specific resource the fix needs
The person you can get a meeting with most easily this week

questions.explanation: The person whose yes changes the least is usually easiest to meet, which is why so many proposals stop at the wrong desk.

questions.from: This module — Why Correct Findings Don't Get Fixed
questions.prompt: Which request is sized so that a decision-maker can actually say yes?

options.label: A broad request to prioritise accessibility across the product
A list of each finding in the audit, set out one after another
A named recipient, a specific resource, evidence and a deadline

questions.explanation: A decision-maker can only say yes to something sized small enough to be a decision. "Please prioritise this" has none of the four parts.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: Meeting a team where their process already is
description: A new mandatory meeting nobody has time for gets skipped within a month. A checklist item added to a PR template a team already uses survives — because it costs nothing extra to notice.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish an intervention that adds new process from one that rides an existing one
Fit an accessibility check into a team's existing workflow artefacts rather than proposing new ceremony

contentSections.title: The meeting nobody has time for

contentSections.body: A new reviewer proposes a weekly 'Accessibility Review Meeting.' Six people accept the invite. By the fourth week, two show up. By the eighth, the meeting is quietly cancelled by whoever's calendar it was cluttering — nobody decided accessibility stopped mattering; a new, extra thing simply lost, the way new extra things almost always lose, to everything already running.

contentSections.scenario: Two ways the same reviewer could have introduced accessibility checking to this team. Option A: a new standing meeting, on top of the team's existing ceremonies. Option B: one new required checklist item — 'accessibility: keyboard tested, contrast checked' — added to the pull request template the team already fills in for every single PR.
contentSections.question: Which is more likely to still be happening in six months, and why?

options.label: Option A — a dedicated meeting gives the topic more visible priority
Option B — it costs nothing extra to attend; it rides inside a step the team was already going to do
Neither will last without a dedicated accessibility hire

feedback.meeting: Visibility is real, briefly — a new meeting is highly visible in week one. The problem is durability: every new standing meeting competes against a calendar that's already full, and it's the newest thing on that calendar that gets cut first when the team gets busy, which every team eventually does.
feedback.checklist: Right. A checklist item inside a PR template doesn't ask for a single extra minute of calendar time — it's already there the moment someone opens a PR, exactly like every other line in that template. It doesn't need to win a competition for attention because it was never a separate line item competing for anything.
feedback.neither: A dedicated hire changes what's possible, but the mechanism question here is narrower: given the same person and the same authority, which of these two specific interventions survives contact with a busy quarter. Riding an existing process reliably beats adding a new one, hire or no hire.

contentSections.mechanism: **An intervention that adds new process has to keep winning a fight for time and attention, forever. An intervention that rides an existing process only has to be added once.** The PR template gets filled in whether or not anyone is thinking about accessibility that day — which is exactly why the checklist item survives long after the standing meeting has quietly disappeared from everyone's calendar.

contentSections.body: This generalises past PR templates. Every team already has artefacts and rituals nothing needs to be invented to attach to: a definition-of-done checklist, a design review Slack channel, a QA sign-off step, a release checklist, a component library's contribution guide. Each one already happens whether or not accessibility is on anyone's mind that day. The question worth asking before proposing anything new is: *what does this team already do, every time, that a check could ride inside of instead?*
A new ceremony has to keep winning a fight for time, forever. A check added inside an existing one only has to be added once — and it's usually the difference between a habit and a memory.

contentSections.title: Finding the ride, not inventing the vehicle

contentSections.body: Before proposing anything, the useful first move is a short, honest inventory: what does this specific team already do, every single time, without needing to be reminded?

contentSections.scenario: A team's actual, existing workflow: every PR needs two approvals before merge; every new feature gets a design review in Figma with comments before a single line of code is written; every release has a QA sign-off checklist; there is no regular retro or postmortem process for shipped bugs.
contentSections.question: Which existing step is the strongest candidate to attach a first accessibility check to, and why?

options.label: The PR approval step — a reviewer already has to look at the change closely before approving
Propose adding a new dedicated accessibility retro, since none currently exists
Wait until the team has hired a dedicated accessibility engineer before changing anything

feedback.pr-approval: Right. This step already happens on every single change, with someone already required to look closely enough to approve or not — adding one or two specific things to check for costs that reviewer almost nothing extra, because the close look was already mandatory.
feedback.new-retro: The absence of a retro process might be a real gap worth raising eventually, but inventing a brand-new ritual is exactly the higher-cost, lower-durability move this lesson opened with — there's a cheaper option sitting right there in the existing PR step.
feedback.wait: Waiting for headcount that may or may not arrive means the barrier compounds in the meantime. The PR approval step is available to attach to today, with zero new hires and zero new meetings.

contentSections.concept: **The strongest attachment point is whichever existing step already forces someone to look closely at the work, every time, without exception.** Design review and PR approval both qualify, because skipping them isn't really an option in either team's actual workflow — which means anything attached to them inherits that same reliability for free.

contentSections.body: This is also why the earlier module's advice about entering findings directly into a team's own tracker, rather than a separate document, is the same move at a different scale: in both cases, the goal is to become invisible as extra work and instead show up as a normal part of a step that was always going to happen anyway.
Before proposing anything, ask what this specific team already does, every time, without being reminded — and attach there. A brand-new ceremony is always the more expensive, less durable option.

title: Design review before anything is built
description: A comment in a Figma file, before a line of code exists, is one of the cheapest accessibility fixes an organisation will ever make. The same issue, caught after build, usually means rebuilding — which is exactly why the design stage is worth learning to review directly.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why catching an issue in design review is dramatically cheaper than catching it after build
Review a design file directly for the properties that predict accessibility outcomes before code exists

contentSections.title: The cheapest place to catch anything

contentSections.body: A checkout redesign goes through three rounds of visual review — colours, spacing, copy — and gets approved. Nobody looks at contrast, focus order or error states until QA, six weeks later, when 'add a visible focus state and fix contrast on twelve components' has quietly become a partial re-design instead of a five-minute comment on a Figma frame.

contentSections.scenario: The same accessibility issue — insufficient text contrast on a set of components — caught two different ways: as a comment on the Figma file before any code exists, versus as a bug filed after the components have already shipped to production across a dozen screens.
contentSections.question: Roughly how many times more expensive, in developer time, is fixing it after it's shipped compared to catching it in the design comment?
contentSections.explanation: Estimates vary a great deal by context, and any single number should be held loosely — but the direction is consistently large, commonly cited in the range of five to a hundred times, because of what changes between the two moments: a design-stage fix is one person adjusting one colour value before anything is built. A post-ship fix means finding every place the pattern was already used, changing production code, re-testing each instance, and shipping a new release — and if the low-contrast pattern was copied into other components in the meantime, the count of places to fix has grown too.

contentSections.body: What makes this practical, not just a statistic to quote, is that most of what predicts an accessibility outcome is already visible in a design file, before code exists — you don't need to wait for a working prototype. A reviewable design pass generally covers five things: colour contrast between text and its background (measurable directly from the file's colour values), the implied reading and focus order (does the visual layer order match how a screen reader or keyboard user would actually move through it), target size and spacing for anything tappable or clickable, whether error and empty states are designed at all (not just the happy path), and whether meaning is conveyed by colour alone anywhere in the frame.
Most of what predicts an accessibility outcome — contrast, order, target size, missing states, colour-only meaning — is already checkable in a design file before a line of code exists.

contentSections.title: The comment that gets acted on

contentSections.body: Two comments left on the same Figma frame. One gets resolved in an afternoon. The other sits unresolved for three weeks, because nobody is quite sure what it's actually asking for.

contentSections.code:
Comment left on frame "Checkout — Step 2":

"This isn't very accessible, contrast
 looks low in a few places. Please review
 against WCAG before dev starts."
contentSections.question: What's the actual flaw in this comment, given it's being left in the exact tool and moment where a fix is cheapest?

options.label: It doesn't name which elements, what the measured contrast actually is, or what value would pass — a designer can't act on it without redoing the measurement themselves
It should cite the exact WCAG success criterion number
It's too blunt in tone and should be softened

feedback.no-specifics: Right — and this is the same gap module one's severity work named for written findings, showing up again at design-review speed. 'A few places' and 'looks low' give a designer nothing to click on or measure against; they have to redo your review before they can even start theirs.
feedback.no-citation: A citation adds authority to the claim but still doesn't tell a designer which specific text-on-background pair is low, what it currently measures, or what value would pass — the comment would still be unactionable with a citation added.
feedback.tone: Tone is worth caring about generally, but it isn't what's stopping this comment from being acted on — a perfectly warm version of the same vague comment would sit unresolved just as long.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A design-review comment that gets resolved fast names the exact layer or element, states the measured value, and states the target: *"'Continue to payment' button text (layer: btn-continue-label) is #9A9A9A on #F2F2F2 — measures 2.1:1. Needs 4.5:1 for this text size; try darkening to roughly #595959 or darker."* That's something a designer can act on in the same minute they read it, without reopening a contrast checker themselves to figure out what you meant.

contentSections.body: A design-stage comment that names the exact element, the measured value and the target gets resolved in the file, the same day. A vague one gets read, half-understood, and quietly deprioritised.

title: Pairing with a developer on a fix
description: A written finding tells a developer what's wrong. Pairing on the fix — sharing a screen, showing the exact assistive technology behaviour live — teaches the underlying pattern, which is what stops the same bug reappearing in the next component they build.

learningObjectives.text: Run a pairing session that demonstrates the actual assistive technology behaviour rather than just describing it
Frame a pairing session so a developer experiences it as problem-solving together, not as being corrected

contentSections.title: Showing the bug, not just describing it

contentSections.body: A written finding says: 'Focus is not trapped inside the modal; Tab moves to the page behind it.' A developer reads this, nods, and fixes something adjacent but not quite right, because reading about a focus trap and watching one happen live, with your own hands on the Tab key, are different kinds of understanding.

contentSections.problem: You're pairing with a developer on the modal focus-trap finding above. Screen shared, both able to see the browser. Walk through the session.

steps.label: Reproduce it live, narrating what you're doing
steps.work: "I'm opening the modal now, and pressing Tab five times." Focus visibly moves past the modal's own buttons and onto a search input in the header behind it, still visually covered by the modal overlay.
steps.why: Watching focus land somewhere visually impossible — behind a modal that's still covering the screen — makes the bug immediately obvious in a way the written sentence 'focus is not trapped' doesn't quite land until you've seen it.

steps.label: Ask the developer to predict the fix before offering one
steps.work: "Before I say anything — what do you think needs to happen here?" Often the developer already has a rough idea: something needs to stop Tab from leaving the modal.
steps.why: Same principle as the guess-first pattern in a lesson: a developer who predicts first, even roughly, retains the explanation that follows far better than one who's just handed the answer.

steps.label: Show the mechanism, not just the patch
steps.work: Explain that a focus trap needs three things: focus moves into the modal when it opens, Tab and Shift+Tab cycle only among the modal's own focusable elements, and focus returns to the element that opened the modal when it closes.
steps.why: A developer who understands the three-part mechanism can implement a focus trap correctly on the *next* modal without you in the room. A developer who was handed one line of code learns nothing transferable.

steps.label: Have them make the change while you watch
steps.work: The developer writes the fix themselves, with you available for questions, rather than you writing it and them reviewing it.
steps.why: Muscle memory for where this kind of code lives, and what it looks like, sticks far better when their hands write it. Your job in this step is mostly to stay quiet and let them work.

steps.label: Retest together, live
steps.work: Tab through the modal again, together, confirming focus now cycles inside it and returns correctly on close.
steps.why: This closes the loop the same way a real retest does — verifying the exact original expected behaviour, not just trusting that the code looks different now.

faded.problem: Now pair on a different bug in the same product: an accordion component where clicking a header does expand the content visually, but a screen reader user gets no indication anything changed — no announcement, and `aria-expanded` isn't updated.

blanks.prompt: What should you do first, before explaining anything? (a few words)
accept: show it live
demonstrate it live
reproduce the bug live
blanks.why: Same as before — showing the actual missing announcement with a screen reader running is more convincing and more memorable than describing it.

blanks.prompt: What should you ask the developer before offering the fix?
blanks.answer: what they think the fix is
accept: to predict the fix
what needs to change
their guess at the fix
blanks.why: Prediction before explanation, every time — it's the same mechanism whether you're teaching a learner in a lesson or a developer at their desk.

blanks.prompt: What's the underlying mechanism to explain, not just the one-line patch? (name the attribute plus what should happen)
blanks.answer: aria-expanded must update to reflect the actual open/closed state, and it should be on the toggle control itself
accept: aria-expanded needs to toggle true/false with the state
aria-expanded should be set on the button and updated when state changes
blanks.why: Understanding that `aria-expanded` has to track real state, and where it belongs, is what lets the developer get the *next* expandable component right without you.

blanks.prompt: Who should write the actual code change? (one phrase)
accept: the developer, not you
them, while you watch
blanks.why: The same reason as before: their hands writing it is what makes the pattern stick.

contentSections.procedure: **Reproduce live → ask them to predict the fix → explain the mechanism, not just the patch → let them write it → retest together.** Every step exists to make the *next* bug of this kind something they can fix without you, not just this one.

contentSections.body: Pairing on a fix teaches the mechanism, not just the patch — which is what determines whether the next similar bug needs you in the room at all.

contentSections.title: The session that goes sideways, and the one that doesn't

contentSections.body: Same finding, same developer, two different framings for opening the session — and they lead to very different afternoons.

contentSections.title: Opening the pairing session
contentSections.opening: You're about to start a pairing session with a developer on a keyboard-trap finding you wrote up yourself last week. You open your laptop and say hello.

opening.situation: How you open the session sets the tone for the next hour.
opening.question: What do you say first?

choices.label: "So this component traps keyboard focus — pretty basic accessibility miss, let's get it fixed."
choices.consequence: The developer's shoulders visibly drop. The next twenty minutes are quieter and more defensive than they need to be, and two obvious questions go unasked because the room now feels evaluative rather than collaborative.

choices.label: "Want to see something weird? Watch what happens when I just use Tab on this component."
choices.consequence: The developer leans in, genuinely curious rather than braced. When focus visibly does something unexpected, their first reaction is 'oh, that's wild' rather than 'I messed up.'

digging-in.situation: Focus has just visibly jumped somewhere strange. The developer is curious and asks what's actually happening under the hood.
digging-in.question: How do you respond?

choices.label: Walk through why it's happening — a tabindex value that's trapping focus in an unexpected loop — and ask what they think the fix looks like
choices.consequence: The developer proposes a fix that's close but not quite complete. You build on their idea rather than replacing it, and they land on the full solution having done most of the thinking themselves.

choices.label: Take over the keyboard and just make the fix yourself while narrating
choices.consequence: It gets fixed faster this way. The developer watches, nods, and retains very little — the next similar bug six weeks later gets the same fix applied slightly wrong, because they saw it done once rather than doing it themselves.

defensive.summary: The bug gets fixed, but the session teaches the developer to be guarded around you specifically, which makes every future finding land harder than it needs to.
defensive.lesson: Framing a finding as 'a basic miss' turns a shared problem into a personal verdict before any collaboration has even started. The same information, framed as curiosity ('watch what happens'), gets you the same fix and a developer who's more open next time, not less.

fast-but-shallow.summary: This one bug is fixed correctly and quickly. The pattern behind it isn't learned, and resurfaces in a new component later.
fast-but-shallow.lesson: Speed on the single fix traded against transfer of the underlying pattern — worth doing sometimes, under real time pressure, but it's a choice, not a default. Knowing which one you're choosing, and why, is the actual skill.

collaborative.summary: The fix takes a few extra minutes. The developer leaves able to recognise and fix the same pattern independently next time.
collaborative.lesson: Curiosity-framed reproduction plus asking for their prediction before explaining did two things at once: it kept the session from becoming adversarial, and it made the explanation land, because they'd already started reasoning about it themselves before you added anything.

contentSections.body: How a pairing session opens decides whether the next hour is collaborative or defensive — and a defensive developer retains less, however correct the fix turns out to be.

title: Component libraries: fixing once instead of forty times
description: Forty findings that all trace back to the same shared Button component aren't forty separate problems — they're one root cause with forty symptoms. Fixing it there is faster, but only reaches every consumer once each one actually updates to the new version.

learningObjectives.text: Recognise when many separate findings share a single root cause in a shared component
Weigh the real trade-offs of fixing at the component-library level rather than instance by instance

contentSections.title: One root cause, forty symptoms

contentSections.body: Forty findings across an audit, scattered across product pages, settings, checkout and account management, all with the same underlying defect: a missing accessible name on the shared Button component whenever it's used with an icon and no visible text. Filed as forty separate tickets, they read like forty separate bugs.

contentSections.scenario: The forty findings above, all citing different pages but the same root defect in a component used across the product.
contentSections.question: What's the actual shape of this problem, and where should the fix be made?

options.label: Forty independent bugs, each needing a separate fix on the page where it was found
One root cause in the shared component — the fix belongs there, not on each of the forty pages
Forty bugs that happen to look similar, but each page's specific usage still needs its own review

feedback.forty-bugs: Treating it this way means fixing the same code forty times over, in forty different places, with forty chances to fix it slightly differently each time — and every future icon-only button built from the same component will still ship the same defect.
feedback.one-cause: Right. A shared component with a defect produces exactly this signature — one underlying cause, many surface locations. Fixing the component fixes every current use at once, and every future use automatically, the moment consumers update to the new version.
feedback.similar-not-same: It's worth double-checking that every instance really is the same component and not a lookalike built separately — but once confirmed, treating genuinely shared instances as needing forty separate reviews wastes the entire leverage the shared component gives you.

contentSections.mechanism: **When many findings share the exact same defect and trace to the same shared component, the fix belongs at the component, not at each instance.** This is the highest-leverage fix an accessibility reviewer can point to — one change reaches every current consumer and, importantly, every consumer that doesn't exist yet.

contentSections.body: Spotting this pattern is a specific habit: whenever three or more findings share not just a symptom but the same underlying cause, check whether they trace to a shared component before filing them as separate tickets. A report that groups them explicitly — 'Finding 12: missing accessible name on icon-only Button component, affecting the 14 instances listed below' — is both more useful to the team and a stronger demonstration that you understood the actual defect, rather than just noticing its symptoms in a lot of places.
Many findings sharing one root cause in a shared component are one fix, not forty. Group them and point the fix at the component, not at each page where the symptom showed up.

contentSections.title: The fix isn't free, and it isn't instant

contentSections.body: The component gets fixed in the design system's source code within a day of the finding. Six months later, eleven of the forty original instances still show the same defect in production — because fixing the source and shipping the fix to every consumer are two different events.

contentSections.scenario: A shared Button component's accessible-name defect is fixed in the design system's own repository.
contentSections.question: Which of these are true about what happens next, and which are wishful thinking?

items.label: Every product surface using the Button component is automatically fixed the moment the design system's repo is updated
Each consuming team needs to actually update to the new package version before they receive the fix
Getting the fix merged into the design system in the first place usually needs the design-system team's own buy-in and review, not just a pull request from anyone
Once merged and released, the fix requires no further tracking — treat it as fully resolved everywhere

explanation.auto-everywhere: This is the tempting but false version of the story — a fix in a shared library's source code doesn't reach a single production surface until someone downstream actually pulls in the new version.
explanation.version-bump-needed: Right, and this is where a fresh kind of retest tracking is needed: which of the forty original consumers have actually updated their dependency, and which are still pinned to an old version.
explanation.buy-in-needed: A design system usually has its own maintainers and review process, precisely because a bad change there affects everyone at once — the same leverage that makes fixing it there powerful also makes the barrier to changing it higher than a single team's own codebase.
explanation.one-and-done: Treating the merge as the finish line is exactly how the eleven-instances-still-broken outcome in the hook happens — the fix needs to be tracked through to actual adoption, the same discipline the retesting phase taught for any other finding.

contentSections.synthesis: Fixing at the component level is the highest-leverage move available, and it still isn't free: it needs the design system's own buy-in to land, and it needs tracking through to actual version adoption before you can honestly call it resolved everywhere. 'Fixed in the design system' and 'fixed in production' are, once again, two different claims.

contentSections.body: A component-level fix is the highest-leverage move available — and it still needs the design system's buy-in to land, and tracking through to actual adoption before it's fixed anywhere real.

title: Teaching without becoming the only person who knows
description: A team that can only catch accessibility issues while you're in the room hasn't actually gained a capability — it's gained a dependency. What a lightweight, written knowledge trail needs to survive you leaving.

learningObjectives.text: Recognise when a team's accessibility competence is really just dependency on one person
Build a minimal, durable knowledge-transfer artefact a team can use without you

contentSections.title: The bus factor of one

contentSections.body: A reviewer leaves a company after eighteen months of genuinely good, well-liked work. Nothing was ever written down — every decision, every 'why' behind every fix, lived in her head and in Slack threads nobody indexed. Within two quarters, the same defects she'd already fixed once start reappearing in new components, because nobody who's still there knows why the old ones were built the way they were.

contentSections.scenario: Two accessibility programmes, both apparently thriving after eighteen months. Programme A: one skilled reviewer who personally catches almost everything, with deep trust from the team, and nothing written down beyond individual finding tickets. Programme B: a less individually skilled but more average reviewer, with a short written decision log, a living checklist the team updates themselves, and a rotating 'office hours' slot two other people have also run.
contentSections.question: Which programme is actually more resilient, and to what?

options.label: Programme A — the individual reviewer's skill is producing better outcomes right now
Programme B — its knowledge doesn't live in one head, so it survives that person changing roles or leaving
They're equally resilient as long as both people stay in their roles

feedback.programme-a: Programme A's current output may genuinely be stronger — that's a real, separate axis from resilience. The question here is specifically about what survives that one person leaving, and by that measure Programme A has a single point of failure baked into everything it's built.
feedback.programme-b: Right. Programme B has deliberately traded some individual peak skill for redundancy — the knowledge exists in at least three places (the log, the checklist, more than one person's head), so no single departure erases it.
feedback.equal: They'd be equally *productive* while both stay, but resilience specifically means what happens when that assumption breaks — and only one of these two programmes has anything that survives it.

contentSections.concept: **A programme that depends on one person's memory has a bus factor of one — however good that person is, the programme's actual knowledge disappears the day they do.** Durable competence means the knowledge lives in more than one place: written down, and in more than one person's head.

contentSections.body: This isn't an argument against being skilled, or against a team trusting you specifically. It's a recognition that trust and skill, without anything written down, produce a fragile kind of progress — the team looks capable while you're there and reverts the moment you're not, because 'ask her' was never actually a system, just a habit that happened to work.
A team that can only catch issues while you're in the room hasn't gained a capability. It's gained a dependency — and dependencies leave when you do.

contentSections.title: Building the trail that survives you

contentSections.body: None of this needs a wiki nobody reads. It needs three small, boringly maintainable things.

contentSections.intro: Design a minimal knowledge-transfer setup for a team you're working with for the next six months, assuming you won't be there forever.

fields.prompt: What goes in the decision log?
options: Every single finding you've ever written
The handful of non-obvious decisions and their reasoning — why this pattern, why this exception — not routine findings
A copy of the WCAG standard
fields.correctValue: The handful of non-obvious decisions and their reasoning — why this pattern, why this exception — not routine findings
fields.feedback: Routine findings already live in the tracker. What's genuinely at risk of being lost is the *reasoning* behind non-obvious calls — why an exception was granted, why one pattern was chosen over another — which is exactly the kind of thing that otherwise only lives in your head.

fields.prompt: Who should own and update the team's working accessibility checklist?
options: You, so it stays accurate
The team itself, with you reviewing changes rather than authoring them alone
Nobody — checklists get stale and aren't worth maintaining
fields.correctValue: The team itself, with you reviewing changes rather than authoring them alone
fields.feedback: A checklist only you maintain is knowledge still living in one place, just written down instead of remembered. A checklist the team edits themselves, with your review, is knowledge that's actually theirs.

fields.prompt: What reduces the single-point-of-failure risk fastest?
options: Training one designated backup person to run office hours alongside you
Writing a longer onboarding document
Nothing — redundancy isn't realistic with limited time
fields.correctValue: Training one designated backup person to run office hours alongside you
fields.feedback: A second person who's actually run the session, even a few times, is worth more redundancy than any amount of additional documentation nobody has tested against a real question yet.

contentSections.synthesis: A short decision log for the reasoning that would otherwise be lost, a checklist the team owns and edits (not just consumes), and at least one other trained person — none of this requires much time relative to the review work itself, and all of it is what actually determines whether the programme survives you moving on.

contentSections.body: A decision log for the reasoning, a checklist the team owns, and at least one other trained person — that's the whole difference between a programme that's fragile and one that isn't.

title: Practice — Rewrite Seven Findings as Design-Stage Feedback
description: Seven post-build findings, rewritten as the design-stage comment that would have caught the same issue before a line of code existed. No new concepts — this is where the design-review habit stops being something you follow along with and becomes something you do cold.

learningObjectives.text: Translate a post-build finding into the design-stage comment that would have caught it earlier
Identify which stage — design, pairing, or component library — is the right leverage point for a given finding

contentSections.title: Seven drills

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Seven scenarios across meeting a team's process, design review, pairing, component libraries and knowledge transfer. Do them in one sitting or spread across a few — nothing here is timed.
If a drill needed a hint, that's the thing to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Run an Accessibility Review of a Design Before Build
description: Review a real design file before it's built, write comments a designer can act on inside the tool, and state the build cost each catch avoided — the deliverable a client can actually see the value of.

learningObjectives.text: Run a structured design-stage review covering contrast, order, target size, states and colour-only meaning
Write design-review comments specific enough to act on without a follow-up question
State the build cost a design-stage catch avoided, honestly and specifically

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: A design review is worth the most, and is easiest to demonstrate the value of, the moment before anything gets built — because that's the moment you can honestly say what it just saved.

contentSections.title: Review a design before it's built
contentSections.brief: Find a real, pre-build design file to review: a Figma (or similar) file from your own work, a public design file, or — if nothing real is available — a set of realistic screens you mock up yourself in enough detail to actually review (specific colour values, specific component states, not vague sketches). It needs to be detailed enough to genuinely check contrast values and layer order, not just look at layout.
