contentSections.deliverable: A design review with issues caught pre-build and the build cost avoided: a structured pass across at least one full flow, comments specific enough to act on, and an honest build-cost estimate per issue.

stages.title: Run the structured pass
stages.instructions: Go through the flow checking the five things lesson two named: text contrast against background, implied reading and focus order, target size and spacing, whether error and empty states are designed at all, and any place meaning is conveyed by colour alone. Note every issue you find, however small.
stages.checkpoint: You have a list of specific issues, each tied to a specific screen and element — not a general impression of the flow's quality.

stages.title: Write the comments
stages.instructions: For each issue, write the comment exactly as you'd leave it in the design tool: naming the specific layer or element, the measured or observed problem, and a concrete suggested direction — following the pattern from lesson two's spot-flaw. A designer reading only this comment, with no other context from you, should be able to act on it.
stages.checkpoint: Every comment names a specific element and states a specific, actionable target — none read as a general instruction to 'make this more accessible.'

stages.title: State the build cost avoided
stages.instructions: For each issue, write one or two honest sentences on what fixing it here, before build, actually avoided — compared to catching the same issue after the components had already shipped across however many screens they'd likely have been reused on. Where you genuinely don't know the real multiplier, say so rather than inventing a precise-sounding number.
stages.checkpoint: Each cost estimate is grounded in something specific about that issue — how many places the pattern would likely have been reused, how disruptive a post-ship fix would be — not a single generic number copied across every issue.

rubric.criterion: The pass covers all five checkable properties
rubric.meets: Contrast, order, target size, missing states and colour-only meaning are all addressed, not just whichever was most visually obvious.

rubric.criterion: Comments are specific enough to act on without follow-up
rubric.meets: Each names a specific element, the actual problem, and a concrete direction — matching lesson two's worked example, not a vague instruction.

rubric.criterion: Build-cost reasoning is honest, not inflated
rubric.meets: Each estimate is grounded in something specific to that issue; genuine uncertainty is stated as uncertainty rather than papered over with a confident number.

rubric.criterion: At least one finding demonstrates the shared-component pattern from lesson four, if applicable
rubric.meets: Where an issue repeats across multiple instances of the same component, it's flagged and grouped as a shared-cause fix, not filed as separate line items.

rubric.criterion: The review is usable by someone who wasn't in the room
rubric.meets: A designer reading only the document, with no verbal context from you, could act on every comment.

contentSections.body: The value of a design-stage review isn't abstract — it's the specific build cost each catch avoided, stated honestly enough that a client could actually see it.

title: Checkpoint — Working With Design and Engineering
description: Ten questions: six from this module and four from the module before it in this course. Nothing is drawn from other courses. Ungraded, untimed, and getting one wrong just means it comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's process-fit, design-review, pairing, and component-fix ideas alongside the previous module's diagnostic frame, without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Working With Design and Engineering

questions.from: This module — Working With Design and Engineering
questions.prompt: Why does a checklist item added to an existing PR template tend to survive longer than a brand-new standing meeting?

options.label: It rides a step that already happens every time, so it doesn't have to keep winning a fight for calendar time
Meetings are inherently less effective than written checklists
PR templates are reviewed by more senior people

questions.explanation: A new ceremony has to keep winning attention against a full calendar; a check added to an existing, unskippable step only has to be added once.

questions.from: This module — Working With Design and Engineering
questions.prompt: Why is catching an accessibility issue in a design-stage comment usually far cheaper than catching the same issue after build?

options.label: A design-stage fix is one adjustment before anything exists; a post-ship fix means finding every place it shipped, changing production code, retesting and releasing
Designers are paid less than developers
It isn't actually cheaper — the cost is the same either way

questions.explanation: The gap comes from what has to change between the two moments — one colour value in a file, versus production code across every place the pattern already shipped.

questions.from: This module — Working With Design and Engineering
questions.prompt: What's the key difference between pairing on a fix and just fixing it yourself while a developer watches?

options.label: Pairing transfers the underlying mechanism, so the developer can handle the next similar bug alone; watching a fast fix rarely transfers that understanding
There's no real difference in outcome either way
Pairing is always slower and therefore always the wrong choice under any time pressure

questions.explanation: Reproducing live, asking for a prediction, explaining the mechanism, and letting the developer write the fix themselves is what makes the *next* similar bug something they can handle without you.

questions.from: This module — Working With Design and Engineering
questions.prompt: Forty findings all trace to the same shared component. What's true about fixing it there?

options.label: It's the highest-leverage fix available, but each consuming team still needs to update to the new version before it reaches production
It automatically fixes every consumer the moment the component's source code is updated
It should be avoided, since design-system changes need too much sign-off

questions.explanation: Fixing the shared source is the highest-leverage move, and it isn't instant or free — it needs the design system's buy-in, and it needs tracking through to actual adoption by every consumer.

questions.from: Previous module — Why Correct Findings Don't Get Fixed
questions.prompt: Why does raising awareness rarely close an accountability gap on its own?

options.label: People forget campaign messages within a week of seeing them
Campaigns are priced beyond what most teams can afford to run
It leaves job descriptions, reviews and protected time unchanged

questions.explanation: Job description, review criteria and protected time are the load-bearing parts of a role. A campaign can change the mood in the room and leave the gap where it was.

questions.from: Previous module — Why Correct Findings Don't Get Fixed
questions.prompt: Why do fixes kept in a separate quarterly-review spreadsheet usually get scheduled far less often than the same fixes entered as sized sprint tickets?

options.label: They compete rarely, as a whole programme, against work with harder deadlines — instead of ticket-by-ticket, every sprint, against similarly sized work
Spreadsheets are technically inferior to trackers for any purpose
Developers refuse to work on anything from a spreadsheet

questions.explanation: The format and frequency of the competition changes the odds, not the tool itself or developer willingness.

questions.from: Previous module — Why Correct Findings Don't Get Fixed
questions.prompt: What does real ownership of accessibility work require, beyond a values statement?

options.label: A named role with the authority to prioritise the work and the accountability if it doesn't happen
Company-wide awareness training
A badge from a third-party certifier

questions.explanation: A value, a badge or a training completion rate can all exist alongside zero accountability. Real ownership needs a name attached to authority and consequence.

questions.from: Previous module — Why Correct Findings Don't Get Fixed
questions.prompt: A VPAT claims full conformance with no test date, tester or methodology listed. What's the honest read?

options.label: A claim shaped like evidence, with nothing checkable actually behind it
Strong proof of full conformance
Acceptable, as long as the vendor is well-known

questions.explanation: Zero exceptions across dozens of criteria with no way to check who tested what is a tell for theatre, not thoroughness.

questions.from: This module — Working With Design and Engineering
questions.prompt: What makes a design-stage comment get resolved the same day?

options.label: It stays general so nobody feels blamed for the problem
It names the exact element, the value and the target
It arrives after the design is finished and handed off

questions.explanation: A vague comment gets read, half understood and quietly deprioritised. A specific one can be fixed in the file.

questions.from: This module — Working With Design and Engineering
questions.prompt: What turns an accessibility programme from fragile into durable, per the lesson?

options.label: A decision log, a team-owned checklist and a second trained person
One expert who personally answers the team's questions about it
A much longer audit report with far more detail on each finding

questions.explanation: A team that can only catch issues while you are in the room has gained a dependency, not a capability. Writing things down and training a second person is the difference.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: Legal risk, market reach and cost of late fixes
description: Three arguments a budget holder can actually act on — exposure to legal risk, the size of the market a barrier excludes, and how much cheaper a fix is now than after ship — and how to tell which one lands with a specific person before you open your mouth.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish the three budget-holder-legible arguments for accessibility work from arguments that don't translate to a resourcing decision
Select which of the three arguments is likely to land with a specific stakeholder, based on what their role is actually measured on

contentSections.title: Three arguments a budget holder can act on

contentSections.body: A pitch for a remediation budget opens with a moving personal story about a screen reader user who couldn't check out. The finance director nods, looks genuinely moved, and approves next quarter's marketing spend instead — because nothing in the story was shaped like the kind of decision her role actually makes.

contentSections.scenario: A remediation budget request needs to land with whoever actually controls the money. Three different framings of the same underlying need: (1) 'This is the right thing to do for disabled users.' (2) 'We're one complaint away from a lawsuit under [ACCESSIBILITY_LAW] like the one [COMPETITOR] settled last year, and here's roughly what that cost them.' (3) 'Screen reader and keyboard users are roughly 15% of traffic on this page and our checkout conversion rate for them is a third of the site average — fixing it is a plausible revenue lever, not just a compliance cost.'
contentSections.question: Which of these is most likely to move an actual budget decision, and why?

options.label: Framing 1 — it's the most honest and direct statement of why the work matters
Framings 2 and 3 — they translate the need into legal risk and market reach, the categories a budget decision is actually made from
All three are roughly equally effective, since they all describe the same underlying problem

feedback.moral: It's genuinely the most honest framing of *why the work matters to you* — but 'the right thing to do' isn't a category most budget decisions are made in. A budget holder needs the request translated into whatever categories their own role is actually measured against.
feedback.risk-and-reach: Right. Legal risk and market reach are both things a budget holder's own job already requires them to weigh — cost avoided against risk, or investment against a plausible return. The request now speaks the language the decision is already made in, instead of asking the decision-maker to translate it themselves.
feedback.equal: They describe the same underlying need, but they don't land the same way, because they're addressed to different decision categories. A budget holder whose job is measured on cost and risk hears framing 1 as background context, not as an actionable ask — the information didn't change, but its legibility to that specific decision did.

contentSections.concept: **A budget holder's decision is only ever made in the categories their own role is measured against — usually some mix of legal exposure, revenue or market reach, and cost.** A case has to be translated into one or more of those categories to be actionable, not just true. The moral case can motivate you; it rarely moves someone else's budget on its own.

contentSections.body: The third recurring, genuinely actionable argument is the cost curve: a fix caught in design review costs a fraction of the same fix caught after launch, and a fix made *after* a legal complaint or a public incident costs more again — legal fees, an emergency remediation timeline that disrupts other roadmap work, and often reputational cost that's harder to price but very real. Framed this way, the ask isn't 'please care about this' — it's 'the cost of this work only goes up the longer it waits, and here's roughly by how much.'

Legal risk, market reach and the rising cost of a late fix are the three categories a budget decision actually gets made in. The moral case can motivate you — it rarely moves someone else's budget by itself.

contentSections.title: Matching the argument to the person

contentSections.body: The same three arguments don't land equally with every stakeholder — a general counsel and a growth-focused VP of Product are listening for different things, even in the same meeting.

contentSections.scenario: Three stakeholders, each hearing the same accessibility remediation pitch: in-house legal counsel, a VP of Product whose bonus is tied to conversion metrics, and a customer support lead who fields complaints directly.
contentSections.question: Which argument is each stakeholder most likely to weigh heavily, given what their role is actually measured on?

items.label: Legal counsel weighs legal exposure and precedent from similar cases most heavily
The VP of Product weighs market reach and conversion impact most heavily
The support lead is likely to respond strongly to specific, concrete complaint patterns they've already seen directly, more than to an abstract market-size number
The same single framing, unchanged, should be used with all three because switching the emphasis is dishonest or inconsistent

explanation.legal-risk: This isn't manipulation — it's accurate targeting. Legal counsel's job genuinely is to weigh exposure, and a case built around that is both true and legible to them specifically.
explanation.product-reach: Same logic — a VP of Product's job is genuinely about growth and conversion, so a reach-and-revenue framing isn't a trick, it's speaking to what they're actually accountable for.
explanation.support-anecdote: Concrete, already-experienced complaint patterns often land harder with someone close to the day-to-day than an abstract percentage would — not because the number is less true, but because it's less vivid to someone who already has vivid examples of their own.
explanation.one-pitch-fits-all: Leading with the strongest true argument for a given audience isn't dishonesty — every part of the pitch has to remain accurate regardless of who's hearing it. What changes is *emphasis*, not the underlying facts.

contentSections.synthesis: None of this requires three different documents or three different truths — it requires knowing, before the meeting, what a specific person's role actually gets measured on, and leading with the part of an entirely honest case that speaks to it.

contentSections.body: The underlying case stays honest and consistent. What changes with the audience is which true part of it you lead with — matched to what that specific person's role is actually measured against.

title: Why the inspiration argument backfires
description: A moving story about overcoming a barrier can make a room feel good and change nothing — and it can actively work against the case, by turning a systemic, fixable problem into an individual triumph nobody needs to act on.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why an inspiration-framed appeal tends to produce sympathy without action
Reframe a moving personal account as evidence of a systemic, actionable gap rather than an individual triumph

contentSections.title: The story that moves the room and changes nothing

contentSections.body: A company all-hands features a genuinely moving five-minute video: a blind employee describing how they navigate the company's own internal tools despite significant barriers, framed as an inspiring story of resilience. The room applauds. The tools are not fixed. Six months later, the same employee is still working around the same barriers, now also expected to be quietly grateful for the applause.

contentSections.scenario: The video above: genuinely moving, warmly received, and followed by zero change to the actual tools it described.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism that lets this happen?

options.label: Framing the story around individual resilience turns the barrier into evidence of the person's strength rather than evidence of a fixable system failure — so the natural response is admiration, not remediation
The audience simply didn't care enough about the employee
Five minutes wasn't long enough to convey the seriousness of the problem

feedback.individual-frame: Right. When the story is told as 'look how well this person copes,' the emotional payoff — admiration — is already delivered by the time the video ends. There's no unresolved problem left in the room asking to be fixed, because the framing already resolved it, into a compliment.
feedback.didnt-care: The room's genuine, visible emotional reaction argues against this — people were moved. The gap isn't caring less; it's that admiration and remediation are different responses, and the framing only asked for one of them.
feedback.too-short: A longer version of the same framing would very likely produce the same outcome — more admiration, still no action — because the length isn't what's determining the response. The frame is.

contentSections.mechanism: **A story framed around individual resilience delivers its own emotional resolution — admiration — without requiring anyone to act.** The barrier becomes proof of the person's strength rather than evidence of a system that should have been built better. Nothing is left unresolved that demands a decision.

contentSections.body: This is why 'inspiration porn' — a real term used within disability advocacy for exactly this pattern — is criticised by many disabled people themselves, not because the underlying stories aren't real, but because the framing quietly does the opposite of its stated goal: it makes barriers feel like occasions for admiration rather than problems with an obvious, fundable fix. The same true facts, framed around the system instead of the individual, point somewhere very different.

A story framed around individual resilience resolves itself in admiration, with nothing left for the room to act on. The same facts, framed around what the system failed to build, point at a decision instead.

contentSections.title: Reframing the same true story

contentSections.body: Same employee, same underlying facts, a different frame — and a very different next step available to the room.

contentSections.code:
All-hands script, as originally written:

"I want to introduce [NAME], who despite being blind
has found incredible, resourceful ways to work around
our internal tools every single day. Please join me in
recognising this remarkable resilience."
contentSections.question: Keeping every fact true, what's the one reframe that would most change what the room does next?

options.label: Reframe the ending from praising resilience to naming the specific tool gap and the fix it requires — 'here's what we're funding to close it'
Make the story longer and more emotionally detailed
Remove the story from the all-hands entirely, since it can't be told safely

feedback.name-the-gap: Right. Keeping the same true facts but ending on 'here's the specific gap this reveals, and here's what we're doing about it' turns the same moment into an announcement of action rather than a tribute — the room now has something to do besides applaud.
feedback.longer: More detail can deepen the emotional response without changing what kind of response it is — admiration doesn't need more information, it needs a different destination to be pointed toward.
feedback.remove: The story can be told, and told well — the problem was never that it was shared, but how it resolved. Removing it loses a genuinely compelling, true case for the fix; reframing its ending keeps the case and adds the action.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The flaw isn't dishonesty — every sentence in the original script is true. It's that the script's own final line does the emotional work of 'this deserves recognition' instead of 'this deserves fixing,' and a room that's just been told to recognise something has, functionally, already been told the story is over.

contentSections.body: The same true story, ending on the specific fix being funded instead of on praise for resilience, turns a tribute into an announcement — and gives the room something to do besides applaud.

title: Numbers you can defend, and the ones you can't
description: A confident-sounding statistic that falls apart under one follow-up question does more damage than no statistic at all — it hands a skeptical stakeholder a reason to dismiss the whole case. Which numbers survive scrutiny, and how to use an uncertain one honestly instead of avoiding numbers altogether.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a defensible statistic from one that collapses under a single follow-up question
Present a genuinely uncertain number honestly, without abandoning the quantitative case entirely

contentSections.title: The number that becomes the whole objection

contentSections.body: A pitch opens with '15% of the global population has a disability.' A skeptical VP asks, reasonably, 'what percentage of that 15% is affected by the specific barriers we're talking about fixing, on this specific product?' Nobody in the room has that number. The meeting's remaining twenty minutes are spent litigating the opening statistic instead of discussing the actual proposal.

contentSections.scenario: The same pitch, two different opening statistics. Version A: 'Globally, 15% of people have a disability.' Version B: 'In last month's analytics, 4.2% of sessions used a screen reader or keyboard-only navigation, and their checkout completion rate was 31%, against 68% site-wide.'
contentSections.question: Which is more defensible in the room, and why?

options.label: Version A — it's a widely cited figure from a credible source
Version B — it's specific to this product, drawn from this company's own data, and answers the natural follow-up question before it's asked
Both are equally defensible, since both are true statistics

feedback.version-a: It's true and well-sourced, and it's also the wrong scope for this conversation — it says something about the world, not about this product, which is exactly the gap the follow-up question in the hook exploits.
feedback.version-b: Right. It's scoped to the actual product, drawn from data the company already has and can't easily dispute since it's their own, and it pre-answers the obvious 'but does that apply to us' objection before anyone has to ask it.
feedback.equal: Both are true, but truth alone doesn't make a number defensible in a specific room — defensibility depends on whether it's scoped to the actual claim being made, which only version B is.

contentSections.concept: **A defensible number is scoped to the specific claim being made, ideally drawn from a source the audience can't easily dispute — their own data is the strongest version of this.** A true but broadly scoped statistic invites the one follow-up question ('does that apply here?') that can derail the entire pitch, however accurate the number itself is.

contentSections.body: This doesn't mean broad, well-known statistics are useless — they can be genuinely useful as brief context, in a single sentence, before moving immediately to the product-specific number that actually carries the argument. The mistake is leaning the *entire* case on a number that wasn't measured on the thing being pitched, and then discovering that in the room, live, when someone asks the obvious question.

A defensible number is scoped to the specific product and claim, ideally from a source the room can't easily dispute. A broad, well-known statistic can open a pitch — it shouldn't be asked to carry it.

contentSections.title: What to do with a number you're genuinely unsure of

contentSections.body: Sometimes the honest number simply doesn't exist yet — no analytics were ever set up to measure it, and inventing one to sound more confident is exactly the mistake that blows up in the room later.

contentSections.problem: You're pitching a remediation budget for a mobile app with no assistive-technology usage data at all — the analytics were never set up to capture it. You genuinely don't know what share of users are affected. Present the case honestly.

steps.label: Don't invent a precise-sounding number
steps.work: Resist the pull to write '12% of our users' with no real source behind it, just because a specific number sounds more credible than an honest 'we don't know.'
steps.why: An invented number is exactly the kind of claim that collapses the instant someone asks 'where did that come from' — and once one number in a pitch is shown to be made up, every other number in it becomes suspect too.

steps.label: State clearly what you don't know, and why
steps.work: "We don't currently have assistive-technology usage data for this app, because our analytics were never instrumented to capture it."
steps.why: This is more credible, not less, than a confident guess — it shows the gap was noticed and named rather than papered over.

steps.label: Substitute the nearest defensible proxy
steps.work: "Industry-wide app analytics from [a named, credible source] put assistive-technology usage in this category of app at roughly 3–6%. We'd expect to be in a similar range, though we can't confirm that without instrumenting for it ourselves."
steps.why: A named source and an honest range is a real, checkable claim — very different from an invented precise figure with no source at all.

steps.label: Turn the gap itself into part of the ask
steps.work: "Part of what we're proposing includes adding that instrumentation, so next quarter's version of this pitch has our own number instead of an industry proxy."
steps.why: This makes the uncertainty itself actionable rather than just an admission of weakness — it's now part of what the budget buys.

faded.problem: Now a second uncertain number: you don't know the actual legal exposure a specific unfixed barrier creates, because you're not a lawyer and no legal opinion has been sought.

blanks.prompt: What should you avoid doing with this number? (a few words)
blanks.answer: inventing a specific figure or claim
accept: making up a number
stating a legal claim you can't back up
guessing a specific dollar amount
blanks.why: Same principle — an invented legal claim is exactly the kind of thing that collapses under one question from someone who actually knows the area, like the actual legal counsel in the room.

blanks.prompt: What should you state plainly instead?
blanks.answer: that you don't know and it hasn't been formally assessed
accept: that no legal opinion has been sought
the genuine limit of what you know
blanks.why: Naming the real boundary of your own expertise is more credible than a confident-sounding guess outside it.

blanks.prompt: What's the honest, checkable substitute? (name what kind of thing)
blanks.answer: a named comparable case or settlement, cited accurately
accept: a real precedent from a similar company
a cited example, like a competitor's actual settlement
blanks.why: A specific, named, real precedent is checkable and honest, unlike an invented risk estimate for your own company.

blanks.prompt: What could turn this gap into part of the ask itself?
blanks.answer: proposing an actual legal review as part of the request
accept: asking for a proper legal opinion to be commissioned
including a legal review in the proposal
blanks.why: Same move as before — the uncertainty becomes something the budget can actually buy, instead of just a weak spot in the pitch.

contentSections.procedure: **Don't invent a precise number → state plainly what you don't know and why → substitute the nearest honest, checkable source → turn the gap itself into part of the ask.** A genuinely uncertain number handled this way is more credible, not less, than a confident guess.

contentSections.body: An invented precise number is a liability waiting for one follow-up question. Naming what you don't know, substituting an honest proxy, and turning the gap itself into part of the ask is more credible, not less.

title: Writing for the executive who will forward it
description: Most pitches aren't decided by the person who first reads them — they're decided by whoever that person forwards it to next. Writing something that survives being forwarded with no context attached.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why a pitch's real audience is often not the first reader but whoever they forward it to
Write a message that carries its own context, so it survives being forwarded without explanation

contentSections.title: The reader isn't always the decision-maker

contentSections.body: A well-crafted pitch email goes to an engineering director, who reads it, agrees, and forwards it to the actual budget-holding VP with a single line: 'Worth a look — thoughts?' The VP, with no other context, opens an email written entirely for someone who already understood the background.

contentSections.scenario: The forwarded email above, opening with: 'Following up on our conversation last week — as discussed, here's the breakdown you asked for.' The VP reading it had no prior conversation and wasn't the one who asked for anything.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism that makes this email land badly with its real, final reader?

options.label: The email assumes a shared context that its actual, final reader doesn't have, and gives them no way to reconstruct it
The email is too long for a busy executive to read
The engineering director should have written a longer forwarding note

feedback.assumes-context: Right. The email was written correctly for its first reader and then travelled to someone the writer never planned for — 'as discussed' and 'as you asked' both silently assume shared context that the actual decision-maker doesn't have, and nothing in the message tells them what they're actually looking at.
feedback.too-long: Length isn't the actual problem here — a short email making the same context-dependent assumptions would land just as confusingly. The issue is what it assumes the reader already knows, not how much of it there is.
feedback.short-forward: A longer forwarding note from the director would genuinely help, but it's not something the original writer controls, and it's a fragile fix — the message shouldn't depend on someone else supplying context it should have carried itself.

contentSections.mechanism: **A message's real audience is often not its first reader, but whoever that reader forwards it to — and forwarding rarely comes with a full re-explanation attached.** Writing as if the message might travel with only a one-line note means it has to carry its own context: what this is, why it matters, and what's being asked, without assuming any prior conversation.

contentSections.body: This changes what the opening lines of a pitch need to do. The first two or three sentences should work as a complete, standalone summary even for someone with zero prior context: what the situation is, what's being proposed, and what decision is being asked for. Everything after that can go into more depth for a reader who wants it — but the summary at the top has to survive being the *only* thing someone reads, because for the actual final decision-maker, it often will be.

A pitch's real decision-maker is often not its first reader, and forwarding rarely comes with a re-explanation. Write the opening to work as a complete, standalone summary for someone with zero prior context.

contentSections.title: The one-line summary that survives forwarding

contentSections.body: One sentence, tested against a specific bar: could someone who has never spoken to you, reading only this line, understand what's being asked and decide whether to keep reading?

contentSections.code:
Subject: Following up

Hi — as discussed, wanted to share the numbers
we talked through. Let me know your thoughts
when you get a chance!
contentSections.question: This is a real, common shape for the opening of a pitch email. What's wrong with it specifically for a message that might get forwarded?

options.label: It names no specific topic, no specific ask, and assumes a prior conversation the eventual reader may not have had
It's too informal in tone for an executive audience
The subject line should include the word 'urgent'

feedback.no-content: Right. A forwarded version of this email tells its new reader nothing — not the topic, not the ask, not even what 'the numbers' refers to. It was written entirely for someone who was already in the room.
feedback.tone: Tone matters for how a message lands, but this email would fail just as badly if it were rewritten in a more formal register while keeping the same total absence of actual content — 'as discussed, please find the formal figures attached' has the identical problem.
feedback.urgent: Manufacturing urgency in the subject line doesn't fix the underlying gap — a reader who opens an 'urgent' email and still finds no topic or ask is arguably worse off than one who wasn't told it was urgent at all.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A subject and opening line that survive forwarding name the actual topic and the actual ask in plain language: *Subject: Accessibility remediation — requesting sign-off on 2-sprint budget. Body: We've identified 8 blocker-severity accessibility issues affecting checkout, currently blocking an estimated 4% of sessions from completing a purchase. Proposing one engineer at 50% capacity for two sprints to fix them — full breakdown below.* A reader with zero prior context now knows exactly what they're looking at and what's being asked, in the first two sentences.

contentSections.body: Test the opening against one bar: could someone who's never spoken to you, reading only this line, understand the topic and the ask? If not, it won't survive being forwarded.

title: Using your own experience without becoming the exhibit
description: Your own lived experience is real, specific, hard-to-dismiss evidence — and if it's the only evidence in the case, the whole argument can be dismissed the moment someone decides your situation is unusual. Using it as one strong data point among several, not as the entire exhibit.

learningObjectives.text: Recognise when a case is resting entirely on the reviewer's own experience rather than on broader evidence
Use personal, lived-experience evidence alongside other evidence, without letting the case be reduced to 'this one person's situation'

contentSections.title: When the case becomes about you instead of the barrier

contentSections.body: A reviewer, herself a wheelchair user, pitches a fix for an inaccessible office booking system using her own daily frustration as the entire case. A stakeholder replies: 'I hear you, and I'm sorry it's been hard — but we don't have many wheelchair users on staff, so I'm not sure this is a widespread enough problem to prioritise this quarter.' The case is now closed, having become a referendum on how common her specific situation is.

contentSections.scenario: The exchange above: a reviewer's genuine, specific, true lived experience, offered as the entirety of the evidence for a fix.
contentSections.question: What actually went wrong here, given that everything she said was true?

options.label: Nothing — the stakeholder's response was simply dismissive and unreasonable

With her own experience as the only evidence, the stakeholder could reduce the whole case to a question about how many people share her specific situation — a question the case had no other evidence to answer
She shouldn't have disclosed her disability in a work context at all

feedback.stakeholder-fault: The response is genuinely frustrating, and it's also a predictable move available to anyone hearing a case built on one person's account — the fix for that isn't hoping stakeholders behave better, it's not leaving that opening available.
feedback.sole-evidence: Right. When personal experience is the *only* evidence, a stakeholder can always ask 'how many people does this actually affect' and there's nothing else in the case to answer with — the true, specific account becomes the entire, and therefore fragile, foundation.
feedback.shouldnt-disclose: Her disclosure isn't the problem, and this framing risks putting the burden on her rather than on how the case was built. The gap is evidentiary, not personal — the case needed more than one account to stand on, regardless of whether that account was hers.

contentSections.concept: **Lived experience is real, specific, and hard to dismiss on its own terms — and if it's the sole evidence offered, a stakeholder can always reduce the case to a question about prevalence, which personal experience alone can't answer.** It's strongest paired with something else: usage data, other users' accounts, an industry benchmark, a legal precedent.

contentSections.body: This isn't an argument for hiding or downplaying lived experience — it's frequently the most vivid, concrete, memorable part of a case, and concrete beats abstract nearly every time in a pitch. The point is narrower: personal testimony works best as one strong, specific data point that opens the case, paired with something that answers the 'how common is this, really' question the testimony alone can't.
Personal experience is strong, specific evidence — and alone, it invites the one question it can't answer: how common is this, really? Pair it with something that can.

contentSections.title: Building the case around it, not on it alone

contentSections.body: Same reviewer, same true story, rebuilt as one part of a larger case rather than the whole of it.

contentSections.intro: Rebuild the office-booking-system case so the reviewer's own experience opens it, rather than carries it alone.

fields.prompt: How should the personal account be used?
options: As the entire case, told in full detail
As a short, vivid opening example that makes the problem concrete, then handed off to broader evidence
Left out entirely, to avoid the risk
fields.correctValue: As a short, vivid opening example that makes the problem concrete, then handed off to broader evidence
fields.feedback: A short, concrete opening does real work — it makes an abstract accessibility issue vivid and specific — without being asked to also answer the prevalence question on its own.

fields.prompt: What answers the 'how many people does this affect' question the personal account can't?
options: Nothing is needed if the story is compelling enough
Booking-system usage or accessibility-request data, if it exists, or a stated industry benchmark if it doesn't
A promise that more people will be affected in future
fields.correctValue: Booking-system usage or accessibility-request data, if it exists, or a stated industry benchmark if it doesn't
fields.feedback: This is exactly the gap the sole-evidence case couldn't fill — some real number, even an honestly-labelled proxy, closes the opening a stakeholder would otherwise use to dismiss the case as an edge case.

fields.prompt: What should the case close on?
options: A renewed appeal to the reviewer's personal hardship
A specific, sized ask — following the pattern from earlier in this module
An open-ended request to 'take this seriously'
fields.correctValue: A specific, sized ask — following the pattern from earlier in this module
fields.feedback: Consistent with everything else this phase has taught: a case, however it opens, still needs to end on something a decision-maker can actually say yes to.

contentSections.synthesis: The rebuilt case: a short, true, specific opening (her actual daily experience), followed by whatever prevalence evidence exists or an honestly labelled proxy, closing on a sized, addressed ask. The personal story still does real work — it's just no longer the only thing holding the case up.

contentSections.body: A strong case uses personal experience to open, evidence beyond any one person to answer 'how common is this,' and a sized ask to close. None of the three can carry the whole case alone.

title: Practice — Rewrite Seven Weak Arguments for a Budget Holder
description: Seven weak pitches, each missing one specific thing this module named — a defensible number, a decision-shaped close, an audience-appropriate framing. No new concepts: this is where making the case stops being something you recognise and becomes something you can fix cold.

learningObjectives.text: Diagnose which specific gap — framing, evidence, defensibility, audience or closing — weakens a given pitch
Rewrite a weak argument using the module's tools under time pressure

contentSections.title: Seven drills

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Seven scenarios across framing, inspiration-versus-action, defensible numbers, writing for the forward, and using personal experience well. Do them in one sitting or spread across a few — nothing here is timed.
If a drill needed a hint, that's the thing to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Write a Business Case for an Accessibility Programme
description: Write the one-page case you'd actually send: cost, risk and reach translated for a specific named stakeholder, a defensible number, and a specific first ask a real person could say yes to.

learningObjectives.text: Translate an accessibility need into cost, risk and reach framing matched to a specific stakeholder
Use a defensible number and, where necessary, an honestly labelled proxy for one that doesn't exist
Close on a specific, sized first ask a named stakeholder could act on immediately

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: A business case that survives being forwarded, questioned and read cold by someone with no context is a genuinely different document from a good verbal pitch — and it's the one that actually gets a budget moved.

contentSections.title: Write a one-page business case
contentSections.brief: Pick a real or realistic accessibility programme — remediation of a specific product's known findings, or establishing an ongoing review practice — and a real or realistic named stakeholder who could actually fund it. If you don't have a live situation, construct a specific, detailed one from a product and organisation you know well enough to reason about honestly.
contentSections.deliverable: A one-page case with cost, risk, reach and a specific first ask: a case document written for a named stakeholder, using a defensible number, and closing on a sized ask with a deadline.

stages.title: Choose the stakeholder and the framing
stages.instructions: Name a specific stakeholder role and what their job is actually measured against. Decide which of cost, risk and reach — possibly more than one — genuinely fits their incentives, and note briefly why the others would land less well with this specific person.
stages.checkpoint: You've named a specific stakeholder and can state, in one sentence, why your chosen framing fits what their role is measured against.

stages.title: Find or honestly proxy your central number
stages.instructions: Find a number scoped specifically to your product or situation — usage data, complaint patterns, a comparable settlement — that answers the natural 'does this apply to us' question. If a real number genuinely isn't available, follow lesson three's procedure: state the gap plainly, cite an honest named proxy, and consider whether closing the gap belongs in your ask.
stages.checkpoint: Your central number is either genuinely scoped to your own situation, or is explicitly labelled as a proxy with its source named — nothing is stated as fact that you can't actually back up.

stages.title: Write the one-pager
stages.instructions: Write it to survive being forwarded: an opening two or three sentences that work as a complete standalone summary, the framing and number in the body, and a closing ask that's specific, addressed, sized, and has a real deadline — following the pattern from the previous module's decision-maker lesson.
stages.checkpoint: The opening alone would make sense to someone with zero prior context, the number is defensible or honestly labelled, and the closing ask is specific enough for a named stakeholder to actually say yes or no to.

rubric.criterion: The framing matches the specific stakeholder's actual incentives
rubric.meets: Cost, risk or reach is chosen deliberately, with a stated reason tied to what that role is measured against — not a generic, one-size framing.

rubric.criterion: The central number is defensible or honestly labelled
rubric.meets: Scoped to the actual product or situation, or explicitly marked as a named proxy with its source stated, if the real number doesn't exist.

rubric.criterion: The opening survives forwarding with no added context
rubric.meets: The first two or three sentences alone convey the topic and the ask to a reader who's never spoken to you.

rubric.criterion: Personal experience, if used, doesn't carry the whole case alone
rubric.meets: If a personal account is included, it's paired with evidence beyond that one account.

rubric.criterion: The case closes on a specific, sized, addressed ask with a deadline
rubric.meets: Not a general call to prioritise — a named recipient, a sized request, and a date for a response.

rubric.criterion: It fits on one page
rubric.meets: A busy stakeholder could read the whole thing in two minutes.

contentSections.body: A case that survives being forwarded, questioned and read cold is a different document from a good conversation — and it's the one that actually moves a budget.

title: Checkpoint — Making the Case Internally
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from the module before it in this course, and two from the module two back in this course. Ungraded, untimed, and getting one wrong just means it comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's framing, evidence and audience concepts alongside the previous module's process-fit ideas and the diagnostic frame from two modules back, without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Making the Case Internally

questions.from: This module — Making the Case Internally
questions.prompt: What three categories is a budget decision actually made in?

options.label: Legal risk, market reach, and the cost of a fix now versus later
How moving the personal story is, how senior the presenter is, and how long the pitch is
WCAG conformance level, severity rating, and finding count

questions.explanation: A budget holder's role is measured in some mix of legal exposure, revenue or reach, and cost — a case has to translate into at least one of these to be actionable.

questions.from: This module — Making the Case Internally
questions.prompt: Why does a story framed around one person's resilience often fail to produce action?

options.label: It delivers its own emotional resolution — admiration — leaving nothing unresolved for the room to act on
Audiences generally don't care about disabled employees
Personal stories are always too short to be persuasive

questions.explanation: The barrier becomes evidence of the person's strength instead of evidence of a system failure — the same facts, ending on the specific fix instead, point at a decision.

questions.from: This module — Making the Case Internally
questions.prompt: Why is a company's own usage data usually a more defensible opening statistic than a broad, well-known global figure?

options.label: It's scoped to the specific product being pitched and pre-answers the natural 'does this apply to us' question
Global statistics are usually inaccurate
Larger numbers are always more persuasive than smaller ones

questions.explanation: A number measured on the actual product survives the obvious follow-up question a broadly scoped statistic invites.

questions.from: This module — Making the Case Internally
questions.prompt: A pitch email might be forwarded to someone with zero prior context. What should its opening do?

options.label: Work as a complete, standalone summary of the topic and the ask
Save the ask for the end, to keep the reader engaged
Reference the original conversation in detail, to show diligence

questions.explanation: The message's real, final reader may only see the opening lines with no added context — the summary and ask need to be upfront.

questions.from: Previous module — Working With Design and Engineering
questions.prompt: Why does a checklist item added to an existing PR template tend to survive longer than a brand-new standing meeting?

options.label: It rides a step that already happens every time, so it doesn't have to keep winning a fight for calendar time
Meetings are inherently less effective than checklists
PR templates are reviewed by more senior people

questions.explanation: A new ceremony has to keep winning attention against a full calendar; a check added to an existing, unskippable step only has to be added once.

questions.from: Previous module — Working With Design and Engineering
questions.prompt: Forty findings all trace to the same shared component. What's true about fixing it there?

options.label: It's the highest-leverage fix available, but each consuming team still needs to update to the new version before it reaches production
It automatically fixes every consumer the moment the source code is updated
It should be avoided, since design-system changes need too much sign-off

questions.explanation: Fixing the shared source is the highest-leverage move, and it isn't instant — it needs the design system's buy-in and tracking through to actual adoption.

questions.from: Previous module — Working With Design and Engineering
questions.prompt: What's the key difference between pairing on a fix and just fixing it yourself while a developer watches?

options.label: Pairing transfers the underlying mechanism, so the developer can handle the next similar bug alone; watching a fast fix rarely transfers that understanding
There's no real difference in outcome either way
Pairing is always slower and therefore always the wrong choice

questions.explanation: Reproducing live, asking for a prediction, and letting the developer write the fix themselves is what makes the next similar bug something they can handle alone.

questions.from: Previous module — Working With Design and Engineering
questions.prompt: Why is catching an accessibility issue in a design-stage comment usually far cheaper than catching it after build?

options.label: A design-stage fix is one adjustment before anything exists; a post-ship fix means finding every place it shipped, changing production code, retesting and releasing
Designers are cheaper to employ than developers
It isn't actually cheaper

questions.explanation: The gap comes from what has to change between the two moments — one value in a file, versus production code already shipped in several places.

questions.from: Two modules back — Why Correct Findings Don't Get Fixed
questions.prompt: A remediation effort needs two sprints of engineering capacity and a place on the roadmap. Whom should the request go to first?

options.label: The engineering manager, who is closest to the day-to-day work
The VP of Product, who holds roadmap capacity and budget
Legal counsel, because they can require the company to act

questions.explanation: A multi-sprint effort is a roadmap and budget decision. The person to ask is the one who holds the specific resource the fix requires, not the one closest to the work or the one easiest to meet.

questions.from: Two modules back — Why Correct Findings Don't Get Fixed
questions.prompt: Which request is sized so that a decision-maker can actually say yes?

options.label: A named recipient, a specific resource, evidence and a deadline
A broad request to prioritise accessibility across the product
A list of each finding in the audit, set out one after another

questions.explanation: A decision-maker can only say yes to something sized small enough to be a decision. 'Please prioritise this' has none of the four parts.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: Where accessibility fits in a delivery process
description: A single accessibility phase bolted onto the end of delivery is the most expensive place to catch anything and the first thing cut when a deadline compresses. Threading several small gates through a process that already exists survives both problems.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why a single end-stage accessibility phase is structurally the worst place to catch barriers
Place accessibility gates at multiple points in an existing delivery process rather than concentrating them at the end

contentSections.title: The phase that's first to go

contentSections.body: A team adds a single 'Accessibility QA' phase, two days, right before every release. It works, for a while. Then a release gets tight, and the accessibility phase is the one thing cut to hit the date — not because anyone decided it mattered less, but because it's the last gate before ship, and the last gate is always the cheapest-looking thing to skip when the deadline is fixed and everything else is already built.

contentSections.scenario: The single end-stage accessibility phase above, reliably the first thing cut under deadline pressure, release after release.
contentSections.question: What's the actual structural reason this keeps happening, beyond 'the team doesn't prioritise it'?

options.label: A gate placed at the very end of a fixed-deadline process is competing against a date that can't move, with everything else already sunk — it's structurally the easiest thing to cut, regardless of how much anyone values it
The two-day estimate was simply too long for the phase to survive
The team genuinely doesn't care about accessibility, whatever they say

feedback.structural: Right. By the time a single end-stage gate is reached, every other cost is already sunk and the deadline is already fixed — cutting the last remaining step is the only lever left to hit the date, independent of how much the team values what's being cut.
feedback.too-long: A shorter version of the same end-stage phase would face the identical structural pressure — position in the process, not duration, is what makes it the first thing cut.
feedback.dont-care: The same team can genuinely value accessibility and still cut this specific phase under this specific pressure, for the structural reason above — treating it as a values problem misses the actual, fixable mechanism.

contentSections.mechanism: **A single gate placed at the very end of a fixed-deadline process is structurally the easiest thing to cut, because it's the only remaining lever once everything else is already built and the date can't move.** The fix isn't a longer gate or a more senior champion for it — it's not concentrating all the checking at the one point in the process with the least leverage to defend itself.

contentSections.body: This is the same shape of problem the earlier phase named for findings kept in a separate spreadsheet, at a different scale: concentrating something valuable into one place that has to win a single high-stakes competition, instead of distributing it across many small, low-stakes moments that are each individually easy to keep. A delivery process usually already has several places something could be checked — a design review, a PR template, a CI pipeline, a QA pass — each carrying a smaller, more defensible piece of the same responsibility.

A gate positioned at the very end of a fixed-deadline process is structurally the easiest thing to cut. Distributing the checking across several existing, earlier steps removes that single point of failure.

contentSections.title: Threading gates through a real process

contentSections.body: Same team, same product, no new headcount — just moving the checking from one big end-stage phase into four smaller moments that already exist.

contentSections.intro: This team's delivery process already has four stages: design review, PR review, CI pipeline, and a pre-release QA pass. Place a specific, small accessibility check at each one.

fields.prompt: What belongs at design review?
options: A full WCAG conformance audit of the whole design system
A short, specific check: contrast, implied focus order, target size, and whether error/empty states exist
Nothing — design review isn't the right place for this
fields.correctValue: A short, specific check: contrast, implied focus order, target size, and whether error/empty states exist
fields.feedback: This matches what's actually checkable in a static design file, at the moment it's cheapest to fix — a full audit would be disproportionate to a single review, and skipping the stage entirely wastes the cheapest catch available.

fields.prompt: What belongs in the PR template?
options: A required checklist item: keyboard tested, screen reader spot-checked on the changed component
A link to the full WCAG standard for the developer to read
A mandatory sign-off from a dedicated accessibility specialist on every PR
fields.correctValue: A required checklist item: keyboard tested, screen reader spot-checked on the changed component
fields.feedback: A small, specific, doable checklist item rides the PR step that already happens on every change — a mandatory specialist sign-off on every PR would recreate the single-gate bottleneck this lesson opened with, just moved earlier.

fields.prompt: What belongs in the CI pipeline?
options: An automated scanner blocking merge on any violation, treated as full proof of accessibility
An automated scanner catching a defined, honestly scoped set of structural issues, as a regression floor rather than full coverage
Nothing — automation doesn't belong in CI for accessibility
fields.correctValue: An automated scanner catching a defined, honestly scoped set of structural issues, as a regression floor rather than full coverage
fields.feedback: Automation is genuinely useful here as a floor that prevents known-detectable regressions — the mistake, covered later in this module, is treating a green pipeline as proof of full accessibility rather than as one honestly scoped layer.

fields.prompt: What belongs in the pre-release QA pass?
options: A full re-audit of the entire product before every release
A focused manual pass on the specific journeys changed this release, using the assistive technology the earlier phase's fluency work covered
Nothing — if design, PR and CI all passed, QA doesn't need to check anything further
fields.correctValue: A focused manual pass on the specific journeys changed this release, using the assistive technology the earlier phase's fluency work covered
fields.feedback: A focused pass scoped to what actually changed catches what automation and static design review structurally can't — dynamic, runtime behaviour — without re-auditing the whole product every single release.

contentSections.synthesis: Four small, specific checks, each riding a step that already happens, catch more collectively than one large end-stage phase ever did — and no single deadline crunch can remove all four at once the way it could remove the one big gate.

contentSections.body: Several small checks threaded through existing steps outlast a deadline crunch better than one large gate at the end — and together they catch more, because each stage catches what the others structurally can't.

title: Acceptance criteria that include access
description: A story ships, meets every stated acceptance criterion, and is completely unusable by keyboard — because accessibility was never written into what 'done' actually meant for that story. Writing acceptance criteria specific and testable enough to actually enforce it.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why a story can meet all its stated acceptance criteria and still ship an accessibility barrier
Write acceptance criteria that state accessibility requirements specifically and testably enough to be enforced

contentSections.title: Meeting every criterion and still shipping a barrier

contentSections.body: A user story: 'Add a filter panel to search results, with checkboxes for category and price range.' It ships, passes every stated acceptance criterion, gets celebrated in the sprint review — and cannot be operated by keyboard at all, because 'keyboard operable' was never one of the stated criteria, and nobody checking against the story's own definition of done had any reason to notice.

contentSections.problem: Write acceptance criteria for the filter-panel story above that would actually catch the keyboard-operability gap before the story is marked done.

steps.label: Identify the interactions the story actually introduces
steps.work: Opening/closing the filter panel, checking/unchecking checkboxes, applying the filter, and seeing the result count update.
steps.why: Acceptance criteria can only be written specifically once the actual new interactions are named — 'make it accessible' isn't testable against anything.

steps.label: State a testable keyboard requirement per interaction
steps.work: 'The filter panel can be opened, checkboxes toggled, and the filter applied using only Tab, Space and Enter, with no mouse.'
steps.why: This is directly testable — pick up a keyboard, do exactly what the criterion says, and it either passes or it doesn't. That's what makes it enforceable rather than aspirational.

steps.label: State what a screen reader user needs to know
steps.work: 'When the filter is applied, a screen reader announces the updated result count.'
steps.why: Naming the specific thing that needs to be announced, rather than 'the panel should be accessible to screen readers,' gives whoever tests it something concrete to check.

steps.label: State the visible state requirement
steps.work: 'Checked/unchecked state is visible without colour alone, and keyboard focus is visibly indicated on every interactive element in the panel.'
steps.why: This closes two common gaps — colour-only meaning and missing focus indicators — that a purely functional test (does the filter technically work) would never catch.

steps.label: Add it to the story's definition of done, not a separate document
steps.work: These four criteria sit inside the same acceptance criteria list as every other requirement for the story — not a linked accessibility checklist, not a separate ticket.
steps.why: A requirement outside the story's own definition of done is exactly the kind of thing that quietly stops counting once time gets tight — the same lesson the earlier module taught about riding existing process instead of adding a separate one.

faded.problem: Now a second story: 'Add a toast notification confirming an item was added to a cart.' Write the accessibility acceptance criteria.

blanks.prompt: What's the key screen reader requirement for a toast that appears without any user navigation action? (name the mechanism)
blanks.answer: it's announced via a live region
accept: announced automatically via aria-live
uses a live region so it's announced without focus moving
blanks.why: A toast appears without the user tabbing or clicking anywhere — the only way a screen reader user learns about it is a live region announcing it automatically.

blanks.prompt: Should the announcement interrupt what the user is currently doing? (yes/no plus which live region politeness)
blanks.answer: no, it should be polite rather than interrupting (assertive)
accept: polite, not assertive
no — polite announcement
blanks.why: A cart confirmation is useful information, not an emergency — an assertive announcement would rudely interrupt whatever the user was doing; polite queues it to be read at a natural pause.

blanks.prompt: How long should the toast remain, in terms of the acceptance criterion? (what property to specify)
blanks.answer: long enough to be read, or dismissible, not on a fixed short timer alone
accept: dismissible or long enough for someone reading slowly
not disappearing before it can be read
blanks.why: A toast disappearing on a fixed short timer, with no way to recover it, fails anyone who reads more slowly — the criterion should specify this rather than leave timing unspecified.

blanks.answer: in the story's own acceptance criteria, not a separate document
accept: in the same list as the rest of the story's requirements
blanks.why: Same principle as before — outside the story's own definition of done, it's optional in practice, whatever it's called on paper.

contentSections.procedure: **Name the actual new interactions → write a testable requirement per interaction → state what needs to be announced or visible → put it in the story's own acceptance criteria, not a separate document.** A criterion that isn't specific and testable isn't really a criterion — it's a wish.

contentSections.body: A story can meet every stated acceptance criterion and still ship a barrier, if accessibility was never one of the stated criteria. Testable, specific requirements inside the story's own definition of done are what actually get enforced.

contentSections.title: The criterion that can't fail a story

contentSections.body: One acceptance criterion, real and common, that looks like it's doing the job and structurally can't.

contentSections.code:
Acceptance criteria for "Add filter panel to search results":

1. Checkboxes filter results by category and price
2. Result count updates when filter is applied
3. Panel is accessible
contentSections.question: Criterion 3 is common in real backlogs. What's actually wrong with it?

options.label: It isn't testable — nobody can look at the finished panel and determine pass or fail against 'is accessible', so it functions as decoration rather than a real requirement
It should say 'WCAG 2.2 AA compliant' instead of 'accessible'
Accessibility shouldn't be a numbered criterion at all — it should be a separate note

feedback.not-testable: Right. Criteria 1 and 2 can each be checked with a specific action and a specific expected result. Criterion 3 has neither — there's no action to take and no specific pass condition, so whoever signs off on the story has nothing to actually verify, and the criterion quietly stops functioning as a criterion at all.
feedback.wrong-wording: A more formal-sounding standard reference has the identical problem — 'is WCAG 2.2 AA compliant' still gives nobody a specific action to take or a specific thing to check on this one panel.
feedback.separate-note: Moving it outside the numbered list makes the untestability worse, not better — a note is even easier to skip than an unenforceable numbered item, and this lesson's whole point is that anything not inside the enforced definition of done tends not to get enforced.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A workable version replaces criterion 3 with the specific, testable statements from the worked example: keyboard operability of each interaction, what a screen reader announces, and how state is shown without colour alone. Each of those has a concrete action and a concrete pass condition — which is the entire difference between a criterion that gets enforced and one that just gets typed.

contentSections.body: 'The panel is accessible' isn't a criterion — it has no action to take and no specific pass condition. A real criterion states exactly what to do and exactly what should happen.

title: Automated checks in CI, honestly scoped
description: A green accessibility scan in CI is genuinely useful as a regression floor — and treating it as proof the product is accessible is the same compliance-theatre mistake this phase named earlier, just automated. Scoping the check honestly is what keeps it useful instead of misleading.

learningObjectives.text: Explain what an automated CI accessibility check reliably catches and what it structurally cannot
Scope a CI accessibility gate honestly, as a regression floor rather than as proof of full accessibility

contentSections.title: The green pipeline that means less than it looks like

contentSections.body: A team adds an automated accessibility scanner to CI, blocking merges on any detected violation. Six months later, in a leadership update, someone says: 'Our CI has caught zero accessibility violations this quarter, so we're in good shape.' A manual audit the same week finds forty real barriers the scanner structurally cannot detect.

contentSections.scenario: The same automated scanner running in CI on every pull request, catching a defined class of structural markup issues before merge.
contentSections.question: Roughly what share of real accessibility barriers on a typical product would you guess this kind of scanner reliably catches?
contentSections.explanation: Somewhere in the 20–40% range is the honest, commonly cited figure — the same fact this track's earlier work on automated testing established. Scanners are strong on markup properties decidable from the DOM alone (missing alt attributes, broken label associations, invalid ARIA) and structurally blind to anything requiring meaning, layout judgement or runtime behaviour — whether an alt text is actually accurate, whether focus moves correctly after an action, whether a live region announces at the right moment. A green pipeline is real, useful evidence about the roughly one-third it can see. It is not evidence about the rest.

contentSections.body: This is the same mechanism named earlier in this phase for a VPAT with zero listed exceptions: a claim that looks more complete than the evidence behind it actually supports. 'Zero CI violations' and 'zero accessibility barriers' are different claims, and letting the first quietly stand in for the second in a leadership update is compliance theatre with better tooling — the intent doesn't need to be dishonest for the effect to be.

A green automated pipeline is real evidence about the roughly one-third of barriers a scanner can structurally detect. Presenting it as evidence the product is accessible is the same theatre this phase named earlier, just automated.

contentSections.title: Scoping the gate honestly

contentSections.body: None of this is an argument against the CI gate — it's an argument for describing it accurately, in exactly one or two sentences, everywhere it gets mentioned.

contentSections.scenario: A team is writing the internal documentation for their new CI accessibility gate — what it does, and what it's for.
contentSections.question: Which of these statements belong in that documentation, and which oversell what the gate actually does?

items.label: "This gate catches a defined set of structural markup issues automatically, and blocks known regressions from merging"
"Passing this gate means the change is WCAG compliant"
"This gate complements, and doesn't replace, the manual and design-stage checks earlier in the process"
"Once this gate passes, no further accessibility testing is needed before release"

explanation.regression-floor: This is accurate and still genuinely useful — it tells the team exactly what confidence the gate buys them, no more and no less.
explanation.full-compliance: This is the exact overclaim the hook's leadership update made — a scanner cannot assess conformance to criteria that require human judgement, and stating it does sets up the same false confidence.
explanation.complements-manual: This is the honest, accurate framing that keeps the gate's real value visible without implying it replaces the design review, PR checklist and QA pass from earlier in this module.
explanation.no-further-testing: This directly contradicts the actual scope of what the tool can detect, and is the specific claim most likely to get quoted back later when a manual audit finds barriers the gate never could have caught.

contentSections.synthesis: The honest version of a CI accessibility gate's documentation is short: what class of issue it catches, and an explicit statement that it's one layer among several, not a substitute for the rest. That's the whole difference between a genuinely useful automated floor and a scanner quietly doing the same job a fake VPAT does.

contentSections.body: Document the gate for exactly what it catches, and say plainly that it complements rather than replaces the manual and design-stage checks. That's the whole difference between a useful floor and quiet overclaiming.

title: Involving disabled users, paid and properly
description: Blindfolding a sighted employee for an afternoon and calling it accessibility testing produces confident-sounding but shallow findings, and quietly stands in for the thing it's simulating. What paying disabled testers properly — for their actual expertise, not just their time — gets right that simulation structurally can't.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why simulating a disability is a weak substitute for testing with someone who actually has adapted expertise using assistive technology
Identify what genuine, ethical involvement of disabled testers requires beyond simply inviting them to participate

contentSections.title: The blindfold isn't the same test

contentSections.body: A well-meaning 'empathy exercise': sighted employees wear blindfolds and try to complete a checkout flow using a screen reader for the first time in their lives. It's genuinely eye-opening for them, and the findings it produces — largely 'this is really hard when you can't see' — are shallow compared to what an experienced screen reader user notices in minutes, because six years of fluent navigation and six minutes of fumbling are not the same instrument.

contentSections.code:
Testing plan, as proposed:

"To validate accessibility before launch, we'll
have 5 sighted employees complete the checkout
flow blindfolded, using a screen reader for the
first time, and note any difficulties they encounter."
contentSections.question: What's the core problem with this plan as a way to actually validate accessibility?

options.label: It measures unfamiliarity with a screen reader rather than whether the product has real accessibility barriers — a fluent user would notice completely different things
5 participants is too small a sample size
Blindfolds are an outdated testing method that should be replaced with newer simulation tools

feedback.wrong-instrument: Right. A first-time screen reader user's struggle mostly reflects unfamiliarity with the tool itself, not the product's actual barriers — they'll likely miss real defects a fluent user would catch instantly, and flag normal screen reader behaviour as a bug simply because it's unfamiliar to them.
feedback.sample-size: Sample size is a real, separate consideration, but it doesn't address the deeper problem — five simulated sessions and fifty simulated sessions would share the same fundamental gap between simulated unfamiliarity and real fluent use.
feedback.outdated-method: A newer or more sophisticated simulation tool would still be simulating rather than measuring lived, fluent expertise — the format of the simulation isn't the actual gap.

contentSections.flawExplanation: Simulating a disability for an afternoon measures what it's like to be new to an assistive technology, which is a real but different thing from what it's like to be a fluent, adapted user of one. A screen reader user with years of daily practice navigates by heading and landmark at speed, has strong expectations about what should be announced and when, and will catch defects a first-time user simply won't notice yet — because they don't yet know what correct behaviour is supposed to feel like. The simulation isn't worthless as an internal empathy exercise; it's the wrong instrument to validate a product's real accessibility.

contentSections.body: A simulated disability mostly measures unfamiliarity with a tool, not a product's real barriers. Fluent, adapted expertise from an actual assistive technology user is a different, sharper instrument — and it's the one that finds what matters.

contentSections.title: What proper involvement actually requires

contentSections.body: Even switching from simulation to real disabled testers can still go wrong — if the involvement itself is done badly.

contentSections.scenario: A company decides to involve real disabled users in testing, moving away from the blindfold exercise. Their plan includes several specific practices.
contentSections.question: Which of these are genuine markers of doing this properly, and which are still corner-cutting?

items.label: Paying testers a real rate for their expertise, not a token gift card, comparable to what any other paid usability research participant would receive
Running the recruitment process itself accessibly — accessible sign-up forms, flexible scheduling, remote options
Asking one disabled employee at the company to informally test everything on an unpaid, as-needed, ad-hoc basis
Recruiting testers across a genuine range of assistive technologies and disabilities relevant to the product, not just one convenient tester standing in for 'the disabled perspective'

explanation.paid-rate: This is the baseline, not a bonus — expertise from lived, adapted experience is real expertise, and treating it as a favour to be thanked for rather than work to be paid for is exactly the pattern worth avoiding.
explanation.accessible-recruitment: If the process for finding and onboarding testers isn't itself accessible, it quietly filters out the people the research is meant to include — the same failure mode the product itself is being tested for, showing up one step earlier.
explanation.one-off-favor: This repeats the earlier module's bus-factor problem in a new place — one person, unpaid, informal, becomes a single point of failure and is being asked to do real professional work for free, on top of whatever their actual job already is.
