explanation.diverse-panel: Disability isn't one experience, and one tester's feedback — however genuine — doesn't stand in for the range of assistive technologies and access needs a real product actually needs to serve.

contentSections.synthesis: Proper involvement means paid, professional, deliberately recruited and genuinely diverse testers — the same standard any other form of paid user research would be held to, applied here without the discount some organisations quietly assume is acceptable for disabled participants specifically.

contentSections.body: Real involvement means paid at a real rate, recruited accessibly, and genuinely diverse across assistive technologies — the same bar any paid user research is held to, not a discounted version of it.

title: Maturity models and where a team actually is
description: A team with no process at all wants to jump straight to continuous testing with paid disabled users every sprint. The leap looks impressive on a slide and produces theatre in practice — a maturity model exists to diagnose the real next step, not the most impressive-sounding one.

learningObjectives.text: Diagnose which stage of accessibility maturity a team is actually at, using evidence rather than aspiration
Propose the realistic next stage for a team, rather than the most advanced-sounding one

contentSections.title: The leap that produces theatre

contentSections.body: A team with no accessibility process at all — no checklist, no CI check, no design review step — announces a goal of 'continuous accessibility testing with paid disabled users, every sprint, starting next quarter.' It sounds serious and well-resourced in the all-hands. Three months later, exactly zero sprints have run any such testing, because the basic scaffolding the ambitious goal depends on was never built.

contentSections.scenario: A simple four-stage maturity model for accessibility practice: **Stage 1 — Ad hoc** (barriers fixed only when someone complains, no process). **Stage 2 — Aware** (basic checks exist — a checklist, some training — but inconsistently applied). **Stage 3 — Integrated** (checks are built into the delivery process at multiple points, as this module has described). **Stage 4 — Optimising** (continuous testing with paid disabled users, metrics tracked over time, proactive improvement). The team above is currently at Stage 1.
contentSections.question: What does this model suggest their actual next step should be?

options.label: Jump straight to Stage 4, since that's the real end goal anyway and starting there sends the strongest signal
Move toward Stage 2 — basic, consistent checks — since that's the step immediately achievable from where they actually are
Stay at Stage 1 until they can fully fund Stage 4, since partial progress isn't worth pursuing

feedback.jump-to-4: This is exactly the pattern from the hook — an aspirational leap that looks impressive announced and produces nothing delivered, because Stage 4 depends on scaffolding (a working process, a design review step, a CI check) that doesn't exist yet to run continuous testing against.
feedback.next-stage: Right. The realistic next step is whatever's actually reachable from where the team currently is — basic, consistent checks — which then makes the *next* leap, toward Stage 3, genuinely achievable instead of aspirational.
feedback.stay-put: Waiting for full Stage 4 funding treats maturity as all-or-nothing, when the whole value of a staged model is that partial, achievable progress compounds — Stage 2 alone is a real, meaningful improvement over Stage 1, worth doing on its own.

contentSections.concept: **A maturity model's value is diagnostic, not aspirational — its job is to name the realistic next step from where a team actually is, not the most impressive stage to announce.** Skipping stages tends to produce the exact compliance-theatre pattern named earlier in this phase: an ambitious-sounding claim with no functioning process underneath it.

contentSections.body: This connects directly back to the module's first lesson: Stage 3, integrated checking threaded through several existing process steps, is precisely what a single end-stage accessibility phase (Stage 1 or 2, dressed up to look more advanced) is not. A team's honest maturity stage is visible in exactly this kind of structural detail — not in how ambitious their stated goals sound, but in what's actually built and running today.
A maturity model's job is diagnosing the realistic next step from where a team actually is, not naming the most impressive stage to announce. Skipping stages tends to produce theatre, not progress.

contentSections.title: Diagnosing honestly, from evidence

contentSections.body: Diagnosing a team's real stage takes the same discipline as diagnosing why an audit stalled, earlier in this phase: evidence, not the team's own stated self-image.

contentSections.scenario: A team describes itself as 'pretty mature on accessibility — we care a lot about it and everyone's aware.' On inspection: there's no written checklist anywhere, no accessibility criterion has ever appeared in a PR template, and the one existing example of a caught issue was found by an external auditor, not by anyone on the team.
contentSections.question: What does the actual evidence support, regardless of the team's self-description?

options.label: Stage 1 (Ad hoc) — caring and awareness exist, but no consistent checks or process do, and the one caught issue came from outside the team entirely
Stage 2 or 3, since 'everyone's aware' is itself a meaningful sign of progress
It's not possible to assess maturity without a formal audit first

feedback.stage-1: Right. Awareness and good intentions, on their own, are exactly what Stage 1 looks like from the inside — the diagnostic evidence for Stage 2 and above is structural (a checklist that actually exists, a criterion that actually appears in the PR template), and none of it is present here.
feedback.stage-2-3: Self-reported awareness is real and worth something, but it's not the same evidence as a checklist, a process step, or an internally caught issue — and this module's whole argument is that the structural evidence, not the stated self-image, is what determines the honest stage.
feedback.cant-assess: A formal audit can add useful detail, but the structural absence of any written checklist or process step is already enough evidence to place this team at Stage 1 — waiting for more assessment before naming the honest starting point just delays the actual next step.

contentSections.mechanism: **A team's honest maturity stage is read from what's structurally in place — a checklist that exists, a criterion in the template, an issue caught internally — not from how the team describes its own culture.** 'We care a lot' is compatible with every single stage; only the structural evidence actually distinguishes between them.

contentSections.body: A team's stated self-image is compatible with any maturity stage. The structural evidence — what checklist, what process step, what's actually caught internally — is what tells you which stage is real.

title: Practice — Place the Right Intervention in Seven Delivery Processes
description: Seven short scenarios, each a real-shaped delivery process missing something specific this module named. No new concepts — this is where designing the right process intervention stops being something you follow along with and becomes something you can do cold.

learningObjectives.text: Diagnose which process gap — gate placement, acceptance criteria, CI scope, user involvement or maturity mismatch — explains a given process failure
Propose the specific, right-sized intervention for a team's actual situation

contentSections.title: Seven drills

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Seven scenarios across gate placement, acceptance criteria, honestly scoped CI, real user involvement, and maturity diagnosis. Do them in one sitting or spread across a few — nothing here is timed.
If a drill needed a hint, that's the thing to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Design an Accessibility Process for One Real Team
description: Diagnose a team's honest maturity stage from evidence, design gates threaded through their real existing process, and write the specific first-90-days plan that's actually reachable from where they are today.

learningObjectives.text: Diagnose a team's real accessibility maturity stage from structural evidence
Design process gates, acceptance criteria and an honestly scoped CI check fitted to a team's real existing process
Write a realistic first-90-days plan sequenced from the team's actual current stage

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: The process design that actually survives contact with a real team isn't the most complete one on paper — it's the one that starts exactly where that team already is.

contentSections.title: Design an accessibility process for one real team
contentSections.brief: Pick a real team you know something about — your own workplace, a past role, a team you've consulted for — or construct a detailed, realistic one if nothing real is available. You need to know, or plausibly determine, their actual current delivery process: what steps exist today, and what structural evidence exists (or doesn't) of accessibility practice.
contentSections.deliverable: A process design with roles, gates, tooling and a first-90-days plan: an honest maturity diagnosis, a set of gates threaded through the team's real existing process, and a sequenced, achievable first-90-days plan.

stages.title: Diagnose the real maturity stage
stages.instructions: Using lesson five's four-stage model, gather the actual structural evidence available to you — existing checklists, process steps, any internally caught issues — and name the team's honest current stage. State your evidence, not just your conclusion.
stages.checkpoint: You've named a specific stage, backed by at least two pieces of structural evidence, not by the team's stated self-image.

stages.title: Design the gates
stages.instructions: Using the team's actual existing process steps (not an idealised four-stage process if theirs is smaller), place specific, small checks at each real step, following lesson one's method. Write at least one specific, testable acceptance-criteria template for a common story type they build. If a CI gate is realistic for them, scope it honestly per lesson three — name what it catches and what it doesn't.
stages.checkpoint: Every gate is attached to a step that genuinely already exists in this team's process, each check is specific enough to actually verify, and any CI gate's real scope is stated honestly.

stages.title: Write the first-90-days plan
stages.instructions: Sequence the changes into a realistic 90-day plan, starting from the team's actual diagnosed stage, not from the most complete version of the design. Name who's responsible for each step, using the roles that genuinely exist on this team (echoing the earlier module's ownership lesson — a step with no named owner isn't really planned).
stages.checkpoint: Every 90-day step has a named role responsible for it, and the sequence starts from the team's real current stage rather than skipping ahead to an aspirational one.

rubric.criterion: The maturity diagnosis is evidence-based
rubric.meets: Names a specific stage, backed by at least two pieces of structural evidence rather than the team's stated self-image.

rubric.criterion: Gates are attached to the team's real existing process
rubric.meets: Every proposed check rides a step that genuinely already happens in this team's actual workflow, not an idealised process they don't have.

rubric.criterion: At least one acceptance-criteria template is specific and testable
rubric.meets: Names a concrete action and a concrete pass condition, matching the pattern from lesson two.

rubric.criterion: Any CI gate is scoped honestly
rubric.meets: States plainly what class of issue it catches and that it doesn't replace manual and design-stage checks.

rubric.criterion: The 90-day plan is realistic, not aspirational
rubric.meets: Sequenced from the team's actual diagnosed stage, with every step assigned to a named, real role.

contentSections.body: A process design that starts exactly where a team actually is, with named owners for every step, is worth more than a more complete design that starts somewhere the team isn't yet.

title: Checkpoint — From Project to Practice
description: Ten questions pulling across this module, the previous one, and the accountability module further back. Ungraded, untimed — a missed question just comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's process-design concepts alongside the previous module's argument-building ideas and earlier accountability concepts

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — From Project to Practice

questions.from: This module — From Project to Practice
questions.prompt: Why is a single accessibility phase placed right before every release structurally the first thing cut under deadline pressure?

options.label: It's the last remaining lever against a fixed date once everything else is already sunk, regardless of how much anyone values it
Teams that use a single end-stage phase don't genuinely care about accessibility
Two-day phases are always too long to survive scheduling pressure

questions.explanation: Position in the process, not duration or values, is what makes a single end-stage gate structurally vulnerable to being cut.

questions.from: This module — From Project to Practice
questions.prompt: A story meets every stated acceptance criterion and still ships an unusable barrier. What's the most likely explanation?

options.label: Accessibility was never written into the story's own acceptance criteria as a specific, testable requirement
Acceptance criteria are generally unreliable regardless of content
The developer deliberately ignored a known requirement

questions.explanation: A requirement outside the story's own definition of done doesn't get enforced by the process that checks the definition of done.

questions.from: This module — From Project to Practice
questions.prompt: What's the honest, defensible way to describe a passing automated CI accessibility gate?

options.label: It catches a bounded, defined class of structural issues and complements, but doesn't replace, manual and design-stage checks
Passing it means the product is fully WCAG compliant
It should be described the same way a completed manual audit would be

questions.explanation: A scanner reliably catches roughly a fifth to two-fifths of real barriers — honest framing states the bounded scope rather than implying full coverage.

questions.from: This module — From Project to Practice
questions.prompt: Why is a blindfolded, first-time screen reader session a weak substitute for testing with an experienced screen reader user?

options.label: It mostly measures unfamiliarity with the tool itself, not the product's real barriers, which a fluent user would notice differently
Blindfolds are an outdated technology
First-time users are always more critical than experienced ones

questions.explanation: A first-time user's difficulty largely reflects unfamiliarity with normal screen reader behaviour, not necessarily a defect specific to the product.

questions.from: Previous module — Making the Case Internally
questions.prompt: What three categories is a budget decision actually made in?

options.label: Legal risk, market reach, and the cost of a fix now versus later
How moving the personal story is, how senior the presenter is, and how long the pitch is
WCAG conformance level, severity rating, and finding count

questions.explanation: A budget holder's role is measured in some mix of legal exposure, revenue or reach, and cost.

questions.from: Previous module — Making the Case Internally
questions.prompt: Why does a story framed around one person's resilience often fail to produce action?

options.label: It delivers its own emotional resolution — admiration — leaving nothing unresolved for the room to act on
Audiences generally don't care about disabled employees
Personal stories are always too short to be persuasive

questions.explanation: The barrier becomes evidence of the person's strength instead of evidence of a system failure that could be fixed.

questions.from: Previous module — Making the Case Internally
questions.prompt: A pitch email might be forwarded to someone with zero prior context. What should its opening do?

options.label: Work as a complete, standalone summary of the topic and the ask
Save the ask for the end, to keep the reader engaged
Reference the original conversation in detail, to show diligence

questions.explanation: The message's real, final reader may only see the opening lines with no added context.

questions.from: Previous module — Making the Case Internally
questions.prompt: Why is a company's own usage data usually a more defensible opening statistic than a broad global figure?

options.label: It's scoped to the specific product being pitched and pre-answers the natural 'does this apply to us' question
Global statistics are usually inaccurate
Larger numbers are always more persuasive

questions.explanation: A number measured on the actual product survives the obvious follow-up question a broadly scoped statistic invites.

questions.from: 3+ modules back — Why Correct Findings Don't Get Fixed
questions.prompt: What does real ownership of accessibility work require, beyond a values statement?

options.label: A named role with the authority to prioritise the work and the accountability if it doesn't happen
Company-wide awareness training
A badge from a third-party certifier

questions.explanation: A value, a badge or a training completion rate can all exist alongside zero accountability.

questions.from: 3+ modules back — Why Correct Findings Don't Get Fixed
questions.prompt: Why do fixes kept in a separate quarterly-review spreadsheet usually get scheduled far less often than the same fixes entered as sized sprint tickets?

options.label: They compete rarely, as a whole programme, against work with harder deadlines — instead of ticket-by-ticket, every sprint, against similarly sized work
Spreadsheets are technically inferior to trackers for any purpose
Developers refuse to work on anything from a spreadsheet

questions.explanation: The format and frequency of the competition changes the odds, not the tool itself.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: Choosing a product and scoping honestly
description: Most capstone audits fail at week one, not week four — by picking something too large to finish. Choosing a scope you can actually complete, and writing the two sentences that stop it sprawling.

learningObjectives.text: Scope a capstone audit to something completable within your real energy budget
Write a scope statement that states what is reviewed, against what, and what is explicitly excluded

contentSections.title: Picking something real

contentSections.body: Week one of the capstone, a reviewer picks their employer's entire public site to audit: a hundred and forty pages, three separate checkout flows, a support portal behind login. Week four, they've covered nine pages and haven't started the report. The audit was never too hard. It was too big to finish, and that was decided in the first ten minutes.

contentSections.scenario: You need to pick one real, public product to audit for this capstone. Here are five candidates.
contentSections.question: Which of these are a workable scope for a capstone you can actually finish?

items.label: Your employer's entire public site — 140 pages, three checkout flows, nobody has agreed you can publish findings about it
A local independent bakery's online ordering site — five screens including a cart and checkout, fully public, no login required
A national government benefits portal — real and important, but 300+ pages sit behind a login you don't have and involve financial forms outside your review authority
A three-page personal portfolio site with no forms, no cart, and no interactive components beyond a mailto link
A regional nonprofit's donation flow — eight screens end to end, entirely public, no login required

explanation.employer_full: Real and worth doing eventually, but not as a capstone with a deadline: too large to finish, and publishing findings about your own employer without agreement is a permission problem, not just a size problem.
explanation.bakery: Right size: a complete task (order something, pay for it) with enough screens to exercise every access method, small enough to finish in the time you actually have.
explanation.gov_portal: The parts you could review are real, but most of the site is gated behind access you don't have, and financial forms are exactly the kind of scope a reviewer profile (from the foundations phase) should flag as needing a co-reviewer, not solo capstone work.
explanation.portfolio: Too small in the other direction. Three static pages with no forms and no interaction give you almost nothing to find — the capstone needs a product with a real task in it.
explanation.nonprofit_donate: Same shape as the bakery: one complete task, a manageable number of screens, nothing gating you out. Either of these is a workable capstone scope.

contentSections.synthesis: The pattern across both workable choices: one complete task, entirely public, small enough that a bad week doesn't sink it, with enough interactive surface that finding nothing would itself be a finding. Size and permission are the two filters — pass both before anything else matters.

contentSections.body: You don't need anyone's permission to review a public site using your own access method — that's just using the product. You do need to think about what happens to what you find. For this capstone, treat your findings as coursework: real, rigorous, and not sent anywhere without a separate conversation. If a product turns out to genuinely interest you enough to want to send the findings on, that's a good problem to have — and a different, later decision.
A capstone that finishes on a small, real product teaches you more than one that stalls on a large, important one.

contentSections.title: Writing the scope statement before you start

contentSections.body: "I'll audit the checkout flow" becomes, three days in, "I'll audit the checkout flow and also the account settings, because I noticed some things." Nobody decided to expand the scope. It just crept, one noticed thing at a time, until the deadline arrived with half of everything covered.

contentSections.intro: Before you touch the product, write the scope statement you'll put at the top of the final report. Build it field by field.

fields.prompt: What, exactly, is being reviewed?
options: "The whole site"
"The donation flow: landing page through payment confirmation, six screens"
"Whatever I have time for"
fields.correctValue: "The donation flow: landing page through payment confirmation, six screens"
fields.feedback: Named, bounded, countable. A reader can check whether you covered what you said you would.

fields.prompt: Which review methods will you actually use?
options: Automated scan, keyboard-only, screen reader, zoom/contrast
"General accessibility testing"
Whatever seems relevant at the time
fields.correctValue: Automated scan, keyboard-only, screen reader, zoom/contrast
fields.feedback: Named methods are checkable and set the reader's expectations for what kind of barrier you could and couldn't have caught.

fields.prompt: Which assistive technology and version?
options: The specific screen reader, browser and OS you'll actually use, with versions
"A screen reader"
Leave it out — it's implied
fields.correctValue: The specific screen reader, browser and OS you'll actually use, with versions
fields.feedback: A finding that only reproduces on one combination is still real, but a reader needs to know which combination you tested to judge how far the findings generalise.

fields.prompt: What is explicitly out of scope, and why?
options: Say nothing was excluded
"Account creation and login — behind a test-data requirement I don't have access to"
Bury it in a footnote
fields.correctValue: "Account creation and login — behind a test-data requirement I don't have access to"
fields.feedback: Stating an exclusion and its reason is what turns a gap into an honest scope decision instead of a silent hole a reader discovers on their own.

contentSections.synthesis: Four sentences, written before you start, do more to keep a capstone finishable than any amount of discipline mid-audit. They're also the first paragraph of the report you'll write in lesson four — you're not writing this twice.

contentSections.body: The scope statement you write before you start is what stops the audit sprawling into something you can't finish on your worst week.

title: Running the audit across your own capacity
description: Planning three straight days for the audit works exactly until day two doesn't happen. Staging the audit by access method, and capturing evidence in the stage where you find it, so a bad day costs you nothing you can't pick back up.

learningObjectives.text: Stage a real audit by access method so each session is self-contained and resumable
Capture evidence during a session rather than reconstructing it afterward

contentSections.title: Staging by access method, not by day count

contentSections.body: "Three straight days for the audit," the plan says. Day one goes fine. Day two doesn't happen — a crash, a bad night, a kid home sick, it doesn't matter which. The reviewer comes back four days later with half a screen reader pass, no keyboard pass at all, and no clean record of which was which.

contentSections.question: You have one product to audit end to end, and no way to guarantee tomorrow will be a good day. Put these stages in the order that leaves you with the most usable, defensible coverage if you have to stop after any single one.
steps: Automated scan pass — fast, low effort, establishes the mechanically-checkable baseline
Keyboard-only pass across every interactive element on every screen
Screen reader pass through the core task, start to finish
Cross-check every finding against your reviewer profile for anything that needs a co-reviewer
contentSections.explanation: The scan comes first because it's nearly free and gives you a checklist of the mechanically-detectable third before you spend any real energy. Keyboard-only comes next because it's structural — most navigation and operability barriers show up there, and it needs focus but not deep assistive-technology fluency. The screen reader pass is the most demanding stage, so it goes when you still have the most capacity left. Zoom and contrast can be done on a lower-energy day, visually, without live interaction. The cross-check against your reviewer profile comes last because it depends on having findings to check. Stop after any stage and you have a coherent, describable slice of coverage — not a half-finished mess with no clean edge.

contentSections.body: This is the same principle from the foundations phase's reviewer-profile lab, applied to a real deadline: stage by access method, and every stage boundary becomes a place you could hand the audit off, publish an interim note, or simply stop for the week without losing what you already have.
Stage by access method, not by calendar day — the calendar doesn't know when you'll have a bad one.

contentSections.title: What to capture as you go, not after

contentSections.body: A reviewer finishes a whole keyboard-only pass, closes every tab, and only then goes to write it up — and realises they didn't note which browser build, or the exact three keystrokes that reproduce issue 14. Redoing it costs a session they don't have to spare.

contentSections.problem: Mid keyboard-only pass on the donation flow's checkout step, Tab lands on a custom "Apply promo code" button. Pressing Enter does nothing — no visible change, no error, no focus move.

steps.label: Name the task
steps.why: Every finding starts with what the person was trying to do, not with the element that failed.

steps.label: Record exact repro steps
steps.work: "On /checkout, tab from the promo code input to the Apply button (7 tabs from page load), press Enter."
steps.why: "Some elements" or "the button doesn't work" is unusable two weeks later, even to you.

steps.label: Record environment
steps.work: "Chrome 124, macOS 14, keyboard only, no screen reader running"
steps.why: A finding that's specific to one environment is still real — but only if you know which environment it was.

steps.label: Capture evidence immediately
steps.work: Screenshot the focused state, timestamp the note
steps.why: Evidence taken in the moment survives a crash between now and the write-up. Evidence you plan to remember later mostly doesn't.

steps.label: Assign a tentative severity
steps.work: "Blocks task — no way to apply a discount by keyboard" → high, pending triage
steps.why: A rough severity now is a placeholder, not a commitment — but it means the next stage starts triaging instead of re-deciding from scratch.

faded.problem: Same pass, next screen. The "Save address for next time" checkbox toggles visually when you press Space, but nothing in the DOM changes and no screen reader announcement would fire.

blanks.answer: Save a shipping address for a future order
blanks.why: Starting from the task, not the checkbox, is what makes the finding usable later.

blanks.answer: On /checkout, tab to the "Save address" checkbox (12 tabs from page load), press Space, inspect the DOM state
accept: Tab to the save-address checkbox and press Space, then check the DOM
blanks.why: Specific enough that someone with no memory of this session could reproduce it.

blanks.answer: Chrome 124, macOS 14, keyboard only, DevTools open to inspect DOM
blanks.why: This finding needed DevTools to confirm — say so, so a reader knows how it was verified.

faded.procedure: Task, repro, environment, evidence, tentative severity — in that order, in the stage where you find it, not reconstructed from memory afterward.

contentSections.body: The finding you don't write down in the stage where you found it is the finding you lose to the next crash.

title: Findings, evidence and severity under real volume
description: Six findings sort themselves in your head. Sixty-three don't. Grouping duplicates by root cause and prioritising by cost to the user rather than by the order you found them — before the volume makes both decisions for you by default.

learningObjectives.text: Prioritise a real volume of findings by cost to the user rather than the order found
Group findings that share a single root cause instead of listing each occurrence separately

contentSections.title: Sixty-three findings, not six

contentSections.body: The full staged pass is done. Sixty-three raw notes sit in a document, in the order they were found, some duplicates, some catastrophic, some barely worth a line. The honest reaction is a small wave of panic — and the fastest way to make it worse is to start writing them up top to bottom, in that order, right now.

contentSections.scenario: Findings 14, 22, 35 and 41 all report the same symptom on four different pages of the donation flow: a "Save" or "Continue" button whose focus outline disappears the moment it's clicked, so a keyboard user loses track of where focus went.
contentSections.question: What's actually going on here, and what does it mean for how you write these up?

options.label: Four separate defects, one per page — write four findings
One root cause in a shared button component, appearing four times — write one finding, four instances
A coincidence — four unrelated teams happened to make the same mistake

feedback.four: It reads that way from the outside, but four identical symptoms on the same interactive element, across pages, is the signature of a shared component, not four independent decisions.
feedback.one_shared: Exactly the pattern from the advocacy phase's component-library lesson: forty findings that trace to one shared component aren't forty problems, they're one problem with forty symptoms. Fixing the button component once fixes all four instances, once every page updates to the new version.
feedback.coincidence: Four unrelated teams don't independently reinvent the exact same missing focus style. Shared visual behaviour across pages that don't share a team is close to always a shared component underneath.

contentSections.mechanism: A single `Button` component in the design system sets `outline: none` with no replacement focus style. Every consumer of that component inherits the defect, which is why it shows up wherever the button is used and nowhere it isn't.

contentSections.body: Report both numbers, honestly: sixty-three instances, roughly a dozen root causes. Neither number alone tells the truth — sixty-three sounds unfixable and a dozen sounds trivial, and the real situation is between them. Grouping by root cause is also how a dozen fixes gets sized for a sprint instead of a quarter.
Sixty-three instances and a dozen root causes are both true. Say both.

contentSections.title: Triage under fog, not perfectionism

contentSections.body: A reviewer spends forty minutes deciding whether a barrier is technically a 1.4.3 or a 1.4.11 violation, while a genuine task-blocking finding two rows up still has no severity assigned at all. The forty minutes felt like rigour. It was avoidance of the harder, more useful call.

contentSections.code:
Triage notes, in progress:

#12 — contrast on the footer legal text, 4.2:1 vs 4.5:1 required.
    Debating: cite as 1.4.3 alone, or also 1.4.11? Checking exact hex values again...

#13 — promo code Apply button does nothing on Enter, no error, no focus move.
    (severity: not yet set)

#14 — icon-only close button has no accessible name.
    Debating: is this 4.1.2 or 1.1.1? Re-reading the criteria...
contentSections.question: What's wrong with how this triage session is being spent?

options.label: Time is going into resolving citations for borderline items while a genuine task-blocker sits with no severity assigned at all
Nothing — getting citations exactly right is the point of triage
Contrast findings should always come first alphabetically

feedback.priority: This is the dangerous quadrant from the foundations phase: a hard blocker with no tidy criterion to hide behind, sitting unassigned, while thirty minutes goes into perfecting the citation on a cosmetic-adjacent contrast issue. Citations matter, but not before severity does.
feedback.citations: Citations matter for the report's credibility, but getting #12's exact criterion right buys nothing if #13 — which stops someone donating at all — ships with no severity and gets buried by volume.
feedback.alpha: Alphabetical or numerical order is exactly the trap: it feels neutral but it's really "whichever order I found them in," which has nothing to do with what they cost a user.

contentSections.flawExplanation: Set a severity on every finding before refining any citation. A rough "blocks the core task" beats a perfectly cited "minor contrast issue" every time a reader has to decide what gets fixed first — and at volume, that decision gets made by default, by whatever's easiest to describe, unless triage does it on purpose.

contentSections.body: Assign severity to everything before you perfect the citation on anything.

title: Writing the report and the remediation plan
description: The report has five readers who each need something different in the first thirty seconds, and the remediation plan only gets scheduled if it competes on the terms the roadmap already runs on. Writing both, in one pass, so neither undoes the other.

learningObjectives.text: Write a report whose structure serves the audit's different readers, not just its author
Turn a remediation backlog into tickets sized and framed the way a sprint process already responds to

contentSections.title: One report, several readers, one pass

contentSections.body: A reviewer writes one long document, findings in the order triage left them. The product owner skims the first two pages looking for what's urgent, doesn't find a clear answer, and puts the whole thing aside. The developer who picks up ticket #13 has to hunt through six pages of prose for the actual repro steps.

contentSections.intro: Assemble the report's structure so each reader finds what they need without reading the whole thing.

fields.prompt: What opens the report?
options: The full list of findings, most recently found first
The scope statement from lesson one, then a short summary of what's blocked and for whom
A restatement of what WCAG is
fields.correctValue: The scope statement from lesson one, then a short summary of what's blocked and for whom
fields.feedback: This is what the product owner and anyone forwarding the report need in the first thirty seconds — coverage, and what's actually at stake.

fields.prompt: How are the findings themselves grouped?
options: By WCAG criterion number
By the order they were found in
By root cause, each with its instance count
fields.correctValue: By root cause, each with its instance count
fields.feedback: This is what makes sixty-three findings legible as a dozen fixes, and it's what a developer or designer needs to see the actual shape of the work.

fields.prompt: What does each individual finding block contain?
options: Task blocked, repro steps, environment, evidence, severity, citation
Just the citation and a one-line description
A screenshot with no other text
fields.correctValue: Task blocked, repro steps, environment, evidence, severity, citation
fields.feedback: Task first, citation last — the order from the foundations phase's finding procedure, unchanged at any volume.

fields.prompt: What goes in an appendix rather than the main body?
options: Methodology, assistive technology versions, and anything explicitly out of scope
The three highest-severity findings
Nothing — everything belongs in the main body
fields.correctValue: Methodology, assistive technology versions, and anything explicitly out of scope
fields.feedback: This is the scope statement from lesson one, expanded — it answers a procurement or legal reader's question without slowing down everyone else.

contentSections.synthesis: Same findings, same evidence, structured so each of the five readers from the foundations phase — product owner, developer, designer, legal, procurement — gets what they need without reading the whole document.

contentSections.body: A report structured for its readers gets read. One structured for its author gets skimmed once and filed.

contentSections.title: Fixes that compete on the roadmap's terms

contentSections.body:
From the advocacy phase's first module: a remediation plan kept as its own separate list competes, as a whole programme, against work with harder deadlines — and loses, almost every time. The same fixes, entered as ordinary tickets sized the way the rest of the backlog is sized, compete instead against feature work of similar size. That fight is one accessibility fixes actually win regularly.

Each remediation item needs what any other ticket in this team's backlog already has: an estimate, and acceptance criteria specific enough to test — the same acceptance-criteria discipline from the advocacy phase's delivery-process module, so "fixed" has one meaning everyone can check against, not five different opinions of what "better" looks like.
A remediation plan that reads like a normal sprint ticket gets scheduled like one. A remediation plan that reads like a separate programme gets deferred like one.

title: Defending your findings under challenge
description: "That's not really a WCAG failure." "How many users actually do that?" "We don't have budget this quarter." Three different challenges that sound like one, and staying in the room long enough for the meeting to end with a remediation plan intact.

learningObjectives.text: Respond to specific pushback on a finding with evidence rather than escalation or retreat
Recognise when a challenge is really about resourcing, not about whether the finding is real

contentSections.title: The three things people actually say

contentSections.body: You present your findings. Someone in the room says, "that's not actually a WCAG failure, is it?" Someone else says, "how many users really do that?" A third person says, "we don't have budget for accessibility this quarter." All three sound like the same objection. None of them are.

contentSections.scenario: Three challenges land in the same review meeting, back to back, about three different findings.
contentSections.question: Which one is actually a resourcing objection wearing a technical costume, not a genuine dispute about whether the finding is real?

options.label: "That's not really a WCAG failure" — about a hard blocker with no single clean criterion
"How many users really do that?" — about a finding you have no defensible number for
"We don't have budget for accessibility this quarter" — said after agreeing the finding is real

feedback.notfailure: This one is a genuine technical dispute, and the foundations phase already gave you the answer: the dangerous quadrant is exactly hard blockers no criterion cleanly names. Write it anyway, and defend it on task impact, not citation.
feedback.howmany: This is where the advocacy phase's lesson on defensible numbers applies directly — use the number you can actually stand behind, or say honestly that you don't have one and argue from severity instead. It's a real question that needs a real answer.
feedback.budget: This is the one that isn't actually about the finding at all — the finding was already conceded. Treating it as a dispute to re-argue wastes the room's patience on a fight that was already won; treating it as a resourcing question, and routing it to whoever actually holds the budget line, is the advocacy phase's whole point.

contentSections.concept: Not every pushback is the same shape. A technical challenge needs evidence. A scale challenge needs an honest number or an honest admission you don't have one. A budget objection dressed as either of those needs to be named for what it is and redirected to the person who can actually decide it.

contentSections.body: Match the response to what's actually being challenged — the finding, the scale, or the budget. They need three different answers.

contentSections.title: Staying in the room
The review meeting
contentSections.opening: You're presenting the top three findings from your capstone audit to the product team that would actually own the fixes.

open.situation: You present finding #1: the promo code button doesn't respond to Enter, blocking keyboard users from applying a discount. The product lead says, "Is that really that common a way to check out?"
open.question: How do you respond?

choices.label: Concede the point and drop the finding to keep the meeting friendly
Explain what the finding actually costs — a keyboard user can complete the whole checkout except this one step, silently — and ask what evidence would answer their question
Get defensive and say the number of users doesn't matter, it's a legal requirement

conceded.situation: The finding is quietly dropped from the plan. Two other findings get similar questions later in the meeting.
conceded.question: What do you do now?

choices.label: Hold the line on the remaining findings using task impact, not user counts you don't have
Keep conceding to avoid further friction

pressed.situation: "Fair," the product lead says, "but we genuinely don't have room this sprint for anything that isn't the Q3 launch."
pressed.question: This is a different objection than the first one. How do you respond?

choices.label: Name it as a scheduling question, not a dispute about the finding, and ask what it would take to get it into Q3's sprint as a normally-sized ticket
Re-argue the severity again, since that's what worked a moment ago

defensive.situation: The room goes quiet. The product lead nods politely and moves the meeting on without agreeing to anything.
defensive.question: The finding is technically unrefuted and functionally dead. What's the lesson?

choices.label: "Legal requirement" is true but doesn't answer the question the product lead actually asked

good.summary: You separated a technical question from a scheduling question, answered each on its own terms, and ended with a specific, sized ask the product lead could actually say yes to.
good.lesson: Most pushback in a review meeting isn't one objection — it's several stacked together. Un-stacking them is most of the work of staying in the room.

mixed.summary: You held some findings and lost others to an unanswered question you could have answered. The plan that leaves the meeting is real, but smaller than it needed to be.
mixed.lesson: A concession made to keep a meeting friendly still costs a fix. Ask what evidence would settle the question before dropping anything.

costly.summary: Either every challenge got conceded, or every challenge got met with a citation instead of an answer. Either way, the meeting ends with less agreed than what walked in the door.
costly.lesson: "It's a legal requirement" and silent capitulation are both ways of not answering the actual question in the room. Neither leaves you with a plan.

contentSections.body: The goal in the room isn't winning the argument. It's still having a remediation plan when the meeting ends.

title: Practice — Defend Seven of Your Findings Against Pushback
description: Seven drills on scoping, staging, triage and defence — the skills that turn a pile of raw notes into a report someone actually acts on. No new concepts.

learningObjectives.text: Apply capstone scoping, triage and defence skills to unfamiliar scenarios at speed
Respond to realistic pushback on findings under time pressure

contentSections.title: Seven drills

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Seven drills across scoping, staging, triage, report-writing and defending findings under pushback, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Do them in one sitting or spread across three — nothing expires and nothing is timed.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to rehearse before the actual review meeting — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Deliver the Capstone Audit and Remediation Plan
description: The actual deliverable: a complete audit of the product you scoped in lesson one, run across your own real capacity, written up as a report a stranger could act on, with a remediation plan sized to survive contact with a sprint.

learningObjectives.text: Produce a complete audit report, evidence pack and remediation plan for a real product
Self-assess the deliverable against an explicit rubric before treating it as finished

contentSections.title: The capstone

contentSections.body: Everything in this module has been building toward one document: a report someone who has never met you could read, act on, and defend to their own boss. This lab is where the five lessons stop being separate skills and become one deliverable.

contentSections.title: The capstone audit and remediation plan
contentSections.brief: You have a real, public product and a scope statement from lesson one. Run the audit, triage what you find, and write the document a product team would actually receive: a report, an evidence pack, a prioritised backlog, and a remediation plan sized for a real sprint.
contentSections.deliverable: A complete audit report, evidence pack, prioritised backlog and remediation plan.

stages.title: Finalise scope and inventory
stages.instructions: Confirm the scope statement from lesson one is still accurate — product, methods, assistive technology and version, explicit exclusions. List which review-authority tier (from your foundations-phase reviewer profile) each planned method falls into, and flag anything that needs a co-reviewer you don't have, now, before you start.
stages.checkpoint: You have a final scope statement and a list of any planned methods that exceed your own review authority.

stages.title: Run the staged audit
stages.instructions: Work through the stage order from lesson two — scan, keyboard-only, screen reader, zoom/contrast — capturing task, repro steps, environment, evidence and a tentative severity for each finding as you go, in the stage where you find it. This stage can span more than one real session; treat each stage boundary as a safe place to stop.
stages.checkpoint: Every stage you completed has a self-contained set of findings with evidence captured at the time, not reconstructed afterward.

stages.title: Triage and write findings
stages.instructions: Group findings that share a root cause and report both counts (instances and root causes). Assign a real severity to every finding — blocks the core task, degrades but completable, cosmetic — before refining any citation. Write each finding starting from the blocked task, citation last.
stages.checkpoint: Every finding has a severity, duplicates are grouped by root cause, and the highest-severity findings are the ones that actually block the core task, not the ones easiest to describe.

stages.title: Write the report and remediation plan
stages.instructions: Structure the report per lesson four: scope and summary first, findings grouped by root cause, methodology and exclusions in an appendix. Turn the remediation backlog into sized tickets with testable acceptance criteria, framed the way this team's own sprint process already works.
stages.checkpoint: A stranger could read the first page and know what's blocked and for whom, and a developer could pick up any remediation ticket without asking you a follow-up question.

stages.title: Self-check and prepare to defend
stages.instructions: Run the self-check below against your own draft. Then pick the three findings most likely to get pushback in a real review, and write, for each, the specific response you'd give — not just the citation, the actual answer to "is that really that common" or "we don't have budget."
stages.checkpoint: You have a finished report and, separately, three prepared responses to the pushback you expect to actually get.

rubric.criterion: Scope is honest and stated up front
rubric.meets: The report opens with what was covered, what wasn't, and why — before a single finding appears.

rubric.criterion: Findings are evidence-first, not citation-first
rubric.meets: Every finding names the blocked task and who it affects before it names a WCAG criterion.

rubric.criterion: Duplicate findings are grouped by root cause
rubric.meets: The report states an instance count and a root-cause count separately, and neither number is hidden.

rubric.criterion: Severity reflects cost to the user, not the order found
rubric.meets: The highest-severity findings are the ones that block a core task, not the ones that happened to be found first or are easiest to describe.

rubric.criterion: Remediation items are sized and framed as normal tickets
rubric.meets: Each item carries an estimate and acceptance criteria specific enough that a developer could pick it up without asking you anything.

rubric.criterion: You can defend the top three findings under direct challenge
rubric.meets: For the three findings most likely to be pushed back on, you have a prepared, evidence-based response ready — not just the citation you'd fall back on.

contentSections.body: This is the document. Everything else in the track was practice for being able to write this one, once, for real.

title: Checkpoint — Capstone — A Full Audit and Its Aftermath
description: Ten questions pulling across this module, the previous module, and the phase before it. Ungraded, untimed — anything that doesn't come back now returns in a later checkpoint.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve the capstone's core distinctions without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Capstone — A Full Audit and Its Aftermath

questions.from: This module — Capstone — A Full Audit and Its Aftermath
questions.prompt: What are the two filters a candidate product needs to pass before anything else about it matters?

options.label: It's famous and it's free to access
It's small enough to finish and you have permission or ownership to review and discuss it
It has a lot of pages and uses a popular framework

questions.explanation: Size and permission are the two things that sink a capstone in week one — a scope too large to finish, or one where you can't actually act on or discuss what you find.

questions.from: This module — Capstone — A Full Audit and Its Aftermath
questions.prompt: Why does the staged audit order start with an automated scan and end with the screen reader pass in the middle rather than last?

options.label: The scan is cheapest and fastest, so it goes first; the screen reader pass is the most demanding, so it goes while capacity is highest
Alphabetical order of method names
Whichever method the reviewer personally enjoys most goes first

questions.explanation: Staging by cost and demand, not by preference, means every stage boundary is a defensible place to stop — you keep the cheapest, broadest coverage even if a bad day cuts the audit short.

questions.from: This module — Capstone — A Full Audit and Its Aftermath
questions.prompt: Sixty-three raw findings turn out to trace back to about a dozen shared root causes. What should the report say?

options.label: Only the instance count, sixty-three, because that sounds appropriately serious
Only the root-cause count, a dozen, because that's what actually gets fixed
Both numbers, honestly — neither alone tells the truth

questions.explanation: Sixty-three sounds unfixable and a dozen sounds trivial. The real situation is between them, and reporting only one number misleads whichever direction it leans.

questions.from: This module — Capstone — A Full Audit and Its Aftermath
questions.prompt: In a review meeting, someone concedes a finding is real, then says "we don't have budget for accessibility this quarter." What kind of objection is this?

options.label: A technical dispute about whether the finding is real
A resourcing question, not a dispute about the finding — it needs to be named and routed accordingly
Evidence that the finding should be dropped from the report

questions.explanation: The finding was already conceded. Treating a budget objection as something to re-argue technically wastes the room's patience on a fight that's already won; naming it as a scheduling question and routing it to whoever holds the budget line is the actual next move.

questions.from: Previous module — From Project to Practice
questions.prompt: Why is a single accessibility phase bolted onto the end of delivery structurally the worst place to catch barriers?

options.label: It's the most expensive place to catch anything, and the first thing cut when a deadline compresses
End-stage testing catches more issues than earlier testing does
It's not actually a problem — timing doesn't affect cost

questions.explanation: Threading several small gates through a process that already exists survives both problems that a single end-stage phase doesn't: it's cheaper per catch, and there's no single phase left to cut under pressure.

questions.from: Previous module — From Project to Practice
questions.prompt: A story ships meeting every one of its stated acceptance criteria, and is completely unusable by keyboard. What happened?

options.label: The acceptance criteria never stated an accessibility requirement, so 'done' never included it
The developer ignored the acceptance criteria
This can't actually happen if criteria are met

questions.explanation: You can meet every criterion written down and still ship a barrier, if accessibility was never written into what 'done' meant for that story. Acceptance criteria only enforce what they actually state.

questions.from: Previous module — From Project to Practice
questions.prompt: What does a consistently green automated accessibility check in CI actually prove?

options.label: The product is fully accessible
A useful regression floor holds — the mechanically-detectable class of defects hasn't crept back in — and nothing about the rest
Nothing at all; CI checks are worthless

questions.explanation: Treating a green scan as proof of accessibility is the same compliance-theatre mistake, automated. Scoped honestly, as a regression floor, it's genuinely useful — it just isn't the whole picture.

questions.from: Previous module — From Project to Practice
questions.prompt: Why is simulating a disability — blindfolding a sighted tester for an afternoon — a weak substitute for testing with a disabled user?

options.label: It's cheaper, which is the only real downside
It produces confident-sounding but shallow findings, and stands in for the adapted expertise it can't actually replicate
It's equally valid, just less convenient to arrange

questions.explanation: A sighted person wearing a blindfold for an afternoon hasn't developed the years of adapted technique a fluent screen reader user has — the simulation looks like the real thing and misses what the real thing would catch.

questions.from: Older module — Why Correct Findings Don't Get Fixed
questions.prompt: Why does a remediation plan kept as its own standalone list get scheduled less often than the same fixes entered as ordinary sprint tickets?

options.label: A standalone list competes, rarely and as a whole programme, against work with harder deadlines — and loses
Standalone lists are technically harder to read
There's no actual difference in how often either gets scheduled

questions.explanation: The same fixes, sized and entered as normal tickets, compete instead against feature work of similar size — a fight accessibility fixes win far more often than a competition against the entire roadmap at once.

questions.from: Older module — Making the Case Internally
questions.prompt: Why can an inspiration-framed appeal for accessibility work actively backfire?

options.label: It turns a systemic, fixable problem into an individual triumph nobody needs to act on
Stories are never persuasive in a business setting
It's too emotional to include in any report

questions.explanation: A moving story can make a room feel good and change nothing — the feeling of having witnessed something moving can substitute for the harder, more useful feeling of needing to fix something systemic.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure — and it's also how this whole track ends: not with a final test, but with one more thing that stuck.
